8 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
usually have an antenna mounted on the roof or fender. Modern vehicle  
sets can have most of the features of a base station, although power  
output is usually lower. That, and the fact the antenna isn’t mounted  
as high, means they have a shorter range. However, many vehicle sets 
can also be used as base stations, and connecting them to a higher  
antenna will boost their performance. 
Handheld sets are compact, battery -powered units. They range in size  
from tiny models that can fit in a pocket up to larger ones that clip to 
a belt or load -bearing equipment – and you could stretch a point and  
include military backpack radios in this category. The  main  thing  is  
that, while they have lower power output and a shorter range, they can  
be taken anywhere. 
To decide what kinds of radio you need, look at what you plan to be  
doing after the SHTF. Your home or refuge should have a base station; 
that’s probably going to be the hub of your radio network. If you have 
a survival vehicle it’s probably a good idea to put a set in that too. You 
could take a handheld with you, but they don’t usually work very well 
inside a vehicle; the bodywork acts as a partial Faraday cage, 
weakening the signal. On top of that, most of them are too short-range 
to cope with the sort of distances you can cover in a vehicle. 
As for handhelds, having a few of these is very useful. If you’re out  
hunting, looking after livestock or just walking the perimeter of your  
land, a handheld will  let you contact  home if you  need any  help. 
Planning to  work with your neighbors to  secure the  area against 
looters? You’ll need a way for sentries to talk to each other and call for 
backup if intruders appear. 
So, if you want to be able to communicate by radio in a crisis, you’re  
certainly going to need a base station and probably some smaller radios  
too. It’s all down to your personal situation, but having more options  
available increases your chances of being able to communicate if 
anything unexpected happens. For example, if all you have is a base  
station but you’re forced to leave home for some reason, you’re cut off.  
In that  situation, a  vehicle or handheld  set will give  you a  chance  to

source_components.text:
11 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Handheld CB radios are also available. They’re usually larger than  
pocket size, but compensate for that by having the same power output 
as standard CBs. They do have a shorter range because of the smaller 
built-in antenna, but in good conditions and reasonably flat ground  
most of them can reach out two miles or more. 
Many handheld CB sets can also be connected to an external antenna 
and microphone. That means you can have one in your vehicle, plugged  
into the lighter socket and a standard antenna on the roof, and get the  
range of a vehicle set; then, if required, you can disconnect it and take 
it with you on foot. 
CB radios are affordable. You can get a basic but effective set for under 
$60; for example the Cobra 18WXSTII. It doesn’t have all the features  
of a high -end set, but it works fine and can monitor two channels at  
once. For $100 and up you’ll get more functions. Handheld sets start at 
under $40, and for $80 you can get something like the Midland 75-822, 
which doubles as a vehicle set. 
Multi-Use Radio Service 
MURS was authorized by the FCC in 2000, and like CB it doesn’t need  
a license to operate. It only has five channels, in the middle of the VHF 
band from 151.820 MHz to 154.600 MHz. Transmitters are FM, limited  
to 2W output, and have the same antenna height restrictions as CB. 
There’s a wide variety of MURS devices on the market, including base 
station, vehicle and handheld radios. With a good external antenna  
they can manage a range of up to ten miles. The shortage of channels  
is a drawback, though, and for SHTF use MURS is probably not as  
practical as CB.

13 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
antennas, but it also means you can transmit over very long distances. 
Using skywave transmissions  – bouncing the signal off the  upper 
layers of  the atmosphere – it’s possible to  communicate between 
continents. Many amateur bands are also allowed to use much higher 
power output than CB radio, so 200W transmitters aren’t uncommon. 
CB is fine for talking to people across your local area, but amateur  
radio will let you communicate with anywhere in the USA. 
There’s also a huge range of equipment available for amateur radio.  
Basically, you can use any set that can be tuned into a frequency in  
any of the designated amateur bands. CB sets have the 40 channels  
programmed into them; ham radios can be tuned to any frequency  
inside the set’s operating range. Sets range from small handhelds up  
to high-power sets capable of working with huge dipole wire antennas. 
An easy way to get started with amateur radio, once you have your  
license, is to get a UHF/VHF starter kit. These are usually built around 
a radio capable of putting out around 40 or 50 watts, and have 
everything you need to mount it in a vehicle or use it at home. 
Generally you can expect up to a 20-mile range straight out of the box, 
and that can be significantly increased by connecting it to a larger  
antenna. This sort of kit sells for around $300, which isn’t much more 
than a CB set with similar performance, and it’s a lot more flexible. 
The advantage of getting a UHF/VHF radio is that you can get 
handhelds that will operate on the same frequencies. Modern radios  
also let you dial in channels then store them in memory; often you can 
store up to 999. That means you can set up all your radios with the  
same list of channels, making it easy to quickly switch between nets. 
Another thing it’s easy to do is find a free channel to talk on. In a major 
crisis, expect everyone who has a CB radio to be using it. A lot of them 
won’t be very organized, and they’ll be desperately trying to use their 
radio to find out what’s going on, ask for help and probably a million  
other things. With only 40 channels available it’s going to get crowded, 
and you might really struggle to hold a conversation. There are a lot  
fewer radio hams than CB users, and a lot more amateur frequencies  
than CB channels.

17 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
With most modern radios you can pretty much just take them out of  
the box, plug them in or charge them up, and start sending and 
receiving. That’s fine for a hobbyist, but to get the most out of them in 
a SHTF scenario you should do a little more work. 
Preparing a base station 
If you plan to have a base station in your home or survival refuge – and 
it’s a very good idea – you need to make sure it’s going to do its job.  
That job is acting as the hub of your comms network; anyone who’s  
away from home can talk to the base station. If multiple people are out 
doing different things their handheld sets might not be able to talk to  
each other, but the base station can relay messages. 
Obviously that’s only going to work if the base station can always be  
contacted. In the military, radio sets are always manned; you probably 
don’t have enough people to do that. However, you can set things up so  
that, if someone calls home, they’ll get a response as long as somebody 
is there. 
It’s tempting to set up a radio shack in a spare bedroom or even in an 
actual shed, but if you do that who’s going to hear an incoming call?  
You’re much better putting the radio in a room that’s usually occupied, 
generally the living room or kitchen. Many radios can also be connected  
to external speakers; if yours can, consider putting two or three 
speakers throughout the house so someone will notice a call coming in. 
Base stations run on mains electricity, but in a crisis you’re likely to  
lose power pretty quickly. Use the mains while it works, but have a  
backup. If you have an emergency generator, that will power it. If not, 
look into setting up some car batteries to keep the radio running. 
Because an EMP attack is on the list of potential crises, it’s not just the  
mains you need to have a backup for. An electromagnetic pulse can also  
fry antennas, speakers, electronic microphones and power bricks, so  
keep spare ones in a Faraday cage.

18 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Any radios that aren’t being used should be kept in a cage too. Stored  
radios need to be completely disconnected; it’s no use building one 
around the radio when the pulse can hit the antenna and generate a  
heavy current in it. If you can afford a backup radio, store it in a foil - 
wrapped box inside your cage. 
Other preparations 
Most vehicle radios will work with a simple whip antenna stuck to the 
roof with a magnetic mount, but you’ll get much better performance if 
you set up, and wire in, a proper antenna system. Dual antennas can  
make a huge difference to range, and they also make your signal more 
consistent, especially if the antennas are mounted on the front fenders. 
If you won’t be using the vehicle for more than a few hours, take the  
radio out and put it in a cage. Disconnecting it will give some protection  
from EMP, but not enough that you’d want to rely on it. If your radio  
came with a magnetic whip antenna stick that in the cage as well; it  
will do for a backup if the ones you’ve installed get fried. 
Handheld radios, again, should be stored in a cage when they’re not  
being used or charged. It’s best to keep a few spares as well. Basic  
handhelds are so cheap you can afford to buy another set as backups. 
Finally, plan how to use the channels  you  have  available.  Designate  
one as a general chat net that everyone on the net monitors. If anyone  
wants to  have a conversation they can  switch to  a different  channel,  
then back to the chat net when they’re finished.

20 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
There’s only one serious problem with radios, and that’s security.  
Unless you have military-grade encryption, anything you send over a  
radio can potentially be overheard. All it takes is for someone to tune  
into the same frequency as you, and they can sit there quietly and  
listen to every word. If society has collapsed, that’s not something you 
want happening. 
You can’t stop people listening to what you say on the radio, but you  
can make it difficult or impossible to know what you mean. It isn’t hard  
to conceal important information, so even if someone hears you 
discussing your plans they won’t know enough to interfere. Here are  
some things you should never say in clear: 
• Names of places 
• Names of people 
• Map references 
• Times and dates 
• Details of stores and equipment 
The problem is these are exactly the sort of important pieces of 
information that you often want to send over the radio. The trick is to 
find a way of doing that without letting the whole world know what  
you’re saying. There are ways to do just about all of that. 
Callsigns 
A voice on the radio is just that – a voice. Unless someone knows you 
well enough to recognize your voice over the airwaves they don’t know  
who you are, so why tell them? Instead of saying names over the net,  
give everyone a callsign. There’s no need for it to be complicated. A  
simple way to do it is to just use people’s first initial in the NATO  
alphabet, so if your name is Bob you become Bravo on the radio. If  
you’re married to Belinda it doesn’t matter; just be Bravo 1 and Bravo 
2.

21 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Number offsets 
This simple trick works for any numbers. It doesn’t matter if it’s a map 
reference, a time or somebody’s inside leg measurement – an offset will  
conceal the actual number from any listener. All you have to do is  
decide on a number to use as the offset, then add that to the number  
you want to send. If the result is ten or above, knock off the initial one 
– so ten would be sent as zero, and eleven as one. So for example if you  
use an offset of 4 you get: 
Original 
number 
Offset Encoded 
Number 
0  
4 
4 
1 5 
2 6 
3 7 
4 8 
5 9 
6 0 
7 1 
8 2 
9 3 
Offsets need to be changed at least every day, or patterns start to  
appear. It’s a simple code, though, and it makes it a lot harder for a  
listener to guess exactly what you’re talking about.

22 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Spot codes 
Maps marked with spot codes are a simple way to disguise locations.  
They were developed by British Army covert operators in Northern  
Ireland to let mobile teams securely report their location, and they’re 
now used by many militaries and police forces. 
Setting up spot codes is simple. Just get as many copies of  your local  
area map as you need, and a few packs of colored sticky dot labels. Look  
for small ones, about 6mm or a quarter inch in diameter. Use different  
colors for different types of roads. In the British Army blue is used for  
motorways (freeways), because they’re  shown in  blue on maps.  Red 
shows main roads, and so on. Adapt the colors to however roads are  
marked on your local maps. 
Now stick the dots to prominent points on the map. Road junctions are  
good, and so are noticeable buildings beside the road. If you plan to be  
moving around on foot you can also mark points you expect to be going  
through. You should aim to have enough points that, if you told 
somebody the nearest one to you, they should be able to go there and  
find you pretty quickly. 
Once you’ve marked enough spots, number them. On roads, go in  
sequence – if one junction is numbered 41, the next should be 42. Use 
a different sequence for each color of dot, too. Then, when you give a  
location over the radio, combine the nearest dot’s color and number; for  
example, Red 41. If anyone who’s mobile calls each spot as they pass  
through it, you can easily keep track of where everyone is. 
If there isn’t a spot on your exact location but you want to call it in, just 
pick a nearby spot and give an offset from there – “I’m 400 yards  
northeast of Red 41.”

23 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Code names 
If you mention the names of places – whether it’s towns, streets or  
buildings – on the radio, anyone with a map can quickly work  out  
exactly what you’re talking about. The simple solution is to give code  
names to  any location you think you’re  likely to mention. Pick code 
names that are easy to remember and don’t give any clues to  what  
you’re talking about. If there’s a stockyard near you, don’t call it 
Cowtown. Give it a completely unrelated name that nobody’s going to  
guess. 
Be careful when using code names that you don’t give away what they  
mean by how you use them. If everyone knows you were going to the  
stockyard don’t call in when you get there and say “I’m at Bookshelf  
now.” Just tell them you got where you were going. Obviously you need  
to balance keeping people informed against over -using code names, but  
in general the less often you use them the better. 
Cyphers 
When you start talking about cyphers people get visions of Enigma  
machines and decide it’s too complicated. In general they’re right – 
most cyphers are more trouble than they’re worth. If anyone’s trying to  
intercept your messages it’s likely to be a gang of looters with a police 
scanner, or at most low-level federal officials looking for food supplies. 
You’re not going to be up against Alan Turing and his crack Bletchley  
Park codebreakers. 
If you just want to keep what you’re doing secret from low-level 
listeners, you don’t need elaborate machines or complicated code books.  
These aren’t thinks you want to be messing with anyway. They’re slow  
to use and, unless you’re a highly trained signals operator, it’s easy to  
make mistakes. As one small error can garble your whole message, you  
want to avoid that.

24 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
However, there’s a place for simple ciphers that can be used quickly.  
Say you’ve found something interesting but don’t want the whole  
county to know, or you’ve decided to head for a place that you don’t  
have a code name for and that isn’t near any of your spot codes. It’s  
handy to have a way to encode the name, and one easy way to do that 
is with a bigram table. This is just a 10x10 square with a letter in each 
of its cells and numbers down each side. It looks like this: 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 0 
1 L T H L K N P T J H 
2 B D X F B C C W A R 
3 G S A J H L W M V E 
4 R O N E K F O G L T 
5 J I M P D V B Y J T 
6 F C V C U S R I Y U 
7 U O R E M H Y E G D 
8 E Q S K E Y A P G O 
9 N A F W U D Z E T W 
0 I V T M I S P N K B 
The letters in the cells are, roughly, the full alphabet repeated  four  
times, but some of the less common letters – Q, X and Z – only appear  
once, and there  are a few extra Es and  Ts. If you want to  spell out a  
word all you have to do is find each letter somewhere in the table then  
check the numbers on the  top, then the  side of the table and  use those  
as coordinates for the letter. So if you want to send A, there’s one in the  
third column. It’s also in the third  row, so  you  would send that  as 33.  
To avoid anyone doing letter frequency  analysis, if  a letter is repeated  
in the same word find it  somewhere else  in the table next time. So  if  
you wanted to tell  someone you’d found  an aardvark send  33 for the  
first A, then 92, 78 or 29 for the second one. 
Spelling out words with a bigram table can get tedious, so don’t bother 
trying to encypher whole sentences. Just hide the words that could tell 
a listener the details. You’ll also want to change the tables every few  
weeks, or any time one gets lost. Drawing new ones is something you  
can get the kids to do, as long as they understand the simple rules – 
the most important one being that every copy of a table has to be  
identical.

25 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Advanced Message Protection 
The basic methods covered so far will stop casual listeners from 
understanding your communications, but they aren’t enough if someone 
is actively trying to intercept and analyze your messages.  
If you want a higher level of security, you need to go beyond simple 
codes and start thinking in terms of controlled systems . M ethods that 
don’t just hide information, but also verify who you’re talking to and 
whether your network is still secure. 
The One-Time Pad: Unbreakable Encryption  
There is only one encryption method that is considered completely 
unbreakable: the one-time pad. 
Unlike other codes or ciphers, a one -time pad doesn’t rely on patterns. 
Instead, it uses a completely random key that is the same length as the 
message itself. 
To use it: 
• Write your message as numbers (A=1, B=2, etc.)  
• Add the numbers from your secret key  
• If the result is above 26, loop back (27 = 1, etc.)  
• The receiver subtracts the same key to recover the message  
The critical rules are: 
• The key must be truly random  
• It must be used only once  
• Both parties must have identical copies  
• It must be destroyed after use  
Even modern supercomputers cannot break a properly used one -time 
pad. However, it requires discipline — if the key is reused or captured, 
the system fails completely.

26 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Identity Verification Protocols  
In a compromised environment, the biggest risk isn’t just being 
overheard — it’s someone pretending to be part of your group.  
You need a way to confirm identity without exposing it.  
The simplest method is a challenge–response system. 
Example: 
Challenge: “How’s the weather?”  
Correct response: “Looks like rain.”  
Anyone who doesn’t give the exact response is treated as a threat.  
You can also: 
• Rotate phrases daily  
• Use time-based codes  
• Assign emergency override words  
If a response is incorrect or delayed: 
• End communication immediately  
• Switch channels  
• Assume compromise  
Recognizing Compromised Communications  
There are warning signs that your communication system is no longer 
secure. 
Watch for: 
• Responses that are slightly “off”  
• Correct codes used at the wrong time  
• Unusual delays  
• Repeated signal interference  
• Someone asking for confirmation too often  
If you suspect compromise: 
• Stop transmitting

A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Identity Verification Protocols  
In a compromised environment, the biggest risk isn’t just being 
overheard — it’s someone pretending to be part of your group.  
You need a way to confirm identity without exposing it.  
The simplest method is a challenge–response system. 
Example: 
Challenge: “How’s the weather?”  
Correct response: “Looks like rain.”  
Anyone who doesn’t give the exact response is treated as a threat.  
You can also: 
• Rotate phrases daily  
• Use time-based codes  
• Assign emergency override words  
If a response is incorrect or delayed: 
• End communication immediately  
• Switch channels  
• Assume compromise  
Recognizing Compromised Communications  
There are warning signs that your communication system is no longer 
secure. 
Watch for: 
• Responses that are slightly “off”  
• Correct codes used at the wrong time  
• Unusual delays  
• Repeated signal interference  
• Someone asking for confirmation too often  
If you suspect compromise: 
• Stop transmitting

29 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Coded Phrases in Plain Sight 
Sometimes the safest way to communicate is not to hide your message, 
but to disguise it as something ordinary. 
You can create simple phrases that sound natural but carry specific 
meanings. 
Examples: 
  Phrase                                       Meaning 
“We’re out of milk”                  Immediate danger 
“Dinner is late”                             Delay 
“We’re visiting family”        Relocating 
“The car needs fixing”                  Equipment failure 
“Weather looks bad”                  Situation unstable 
“Package arrived”                  Objective complete 
“We’ll stay home today”        Hold position 
The key is consistency. Everyone must understand the meaning 
instantly. 
Dead Drops: Communication Without Contact  
When direct communication is too risky, dead drops allow you to pass 
messages without ever meeting. 
A dead drop is a hidden location where information can be left and 
later retrieved. 
Common types: 
• Magnetic containers under metal surfaces 
• Buried waterproof capsules 
• Hidden compartments in urban areas 
To signal a drop: 
• Chalk marks 
• Moved objects 
• Subtle visual indicators

A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Rules: 
• Never visit at predictable times 
• Never approach directly after sending a message 
• Always assume the location may be watched 
How They Track You (And How to Avoid It)  
Any radio transmission can be located. 
This is done using triangulation: taking multiple directional readings 
and finding where they intersect. 
You don’t need advanced military equipment to do this. Basic tools can 
narrow your position quickly. 
To reduce your risk: 
• Keep transmissions under 5–10 seconds 
• Never transmit from your main location 
• Move after each transmission 
• Avoid repeating patterns 
• Use terrain to block signals 
The longer you talk, the easier you are to find. 
Anonymous Radio Use 
Even without advanced tracking, patterns reveal identity. 
To stay anonymous: 
• Avoid using real names or consistent callsigns 
• Rotate communication times 
• Change locations frequently 
• Use directional antennas when possible 
• Never transmit from your home base 
Your behavior is often more revealing than your signal.

A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Secure Digital Communication 
If digital networks are still available, encrypted apps can provide an 
additional layer of communication. 
Some platforms are designed to resist surveillance: 
• Signal 
• Session 
• SimpleX 
To use them securely: 
• Enable disappearing messages 
• Avoid real names or personal data 
• Do not sync contacts 
• Use them only on dedicated devices 
Digital tools are useful, but should never be your only method. 
Burner Phone Tactics 
Temporary phones can be used for short-term communication without 
linking back to you. 
Basic rules: 
• Purchase with cash 
• Never associate with your identity 
• Keep powered off until needed 
• Never use in familiar locations 
• Dispose of after limited use 
A burner phone is only effective if it remains disconnected from your 
normal life. 
Silent Communication Methods 
There are times when even radio silence isn’t enough, you need to 
communicate without emitting any detectable signal.

A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Options include: 
• Light signals (flashes from windows or mirrors) 
• Hand signals for close-range communication 
• Knock patterns for entry and identification 
These methods are simple, reliable, and impossible to intercept 
remotely. 
The Layered Communication System 
The most secure approach is not relying on one method, but 
combining several. 
A strong system uses three layers: 
• Primary: Radio communication 
• Secondary: Encrypted digital messaging 
• Tertiary: Dead drops and silent signals 
If one layer fails, the others remain functional. 
When Everything Fails 
If all communication breaks down, survival depends on pre-planned 
coordination. 
Establish: 
• Rally points 
• Check-in times 
• Fallback locations 
• No-contact rules 
The most important communication system is the one you set up 
before you need it.

In a crisis you don’t want to be sitting in front of your radio, scanning  
thousands of frequencies in the hope of stumbling across someone you  
want to talk to. Luckily, there are some frequencies that are regularly  
used by preppers and  survivalists; if  you can tune in to them,  you’ll  
soon be in touch with like -minded people. Here are some of the main  
channels you’ll be interested in; keep a copy of this list beside your base  
station, and if you have radios with programmable channel memories  
you probably want to store at least some of these frequencies in them: 
System Channel Frequency Band Description

GMRS 17 462.6000 MHz UHF Survivalist 
PMR 3 446.03125 MHz UHF Survivalist/Prepper 
MURS 3 151.9400 MHz VHF Survivalist/Prepper 
CB AM 3 26.9850 MHz HF Prepper 
CB AM 9 27.0650 MHz HF Emergency

Amateur HAMU3 446.0300 MHz UHF Prepper

Amateur HAM55 146.5500 MHz VHF Survivalist 
Amateur HAM10M 28.3050 MHz HF Survivalist/Prepper 
Amateur HAM20M 14.2420 MHz HF Prepper 
Amateur HAM40M 7.2420 MHz HF Prepper 
Amateur HAM60M 5.3570 MHz HF Survivalist 
Amateur HAM80M 3.8180 MHz HF Prepper 
SAR SAREMT 155.1600 MHz VHF Search and rescue 
Marine MAR 16 156.800 MHz VHF Marine safety 
Marine MAR 72 156.6250 MHz VHF Boat preppers 
Channels marked Survivalist or Prepper (or both) are exactly  what

38 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Alternatives to radios 
Nothing beats radio for communicating over long distances without  
relying on infrastructure you don’t control. Sometimes you might want  
not want to use it, though. If you’re trying to keep a low profile, and  
not let potential hostiles know where you are, pumping out radio  
frequency energy isn’t a great idea. It doesn’t need much in the way of 
advanced SIGINT gear to find out where a transmitter is sending from. 
A simple directional antenna will give a bearing to your location; take 
two bearings from different points and plot them on a map, look at  
where they meet, and that’s where the transmitter is. You might be  
using good security to disguise what you’re saying, but if an enemy can 
find out your location that might be all they need. 
There’s also electronic warfare to consider. If the government decides 
to shut down radio transmissions for some reason, they’re going to get 
shut down. No equipment you can buy on the open market is going to 
stand a chance against military jammers. That’s bad news if you don’t 
have any other way to communicate. It’s always best to have some  
other options available. 
Field telephones 
Armies all over the world still use field telephones. They’re old- 
fashioned and need to be linked together with wire, but they can’t be  
jammed and they don’t give away your position. If you want to be able 
to talk to neighbors they’re ideal. In fact, if you have enough two-core 
wire, they work over amazingly long distances – the US Army’s TA - 
312/PT will send a signal up to 14 miles in wet conditions, and 22 miles  
if it’s dry. This phone can be found in working order on ebay for about 
$100, and runs on two D -cell batteries. If you run out of batteries, don’t  
worry – it also has a sound -powered mode that’s good up to four miles.  
Field telephones like this can be linked in pairs or in a ring. More 
modern ones cost more, but let you call specific phones on the network.

39 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Field telephones are very secure; the only way to intercept the signal  
is to physically attach an intercept device to the wire. They also can’t  
be jammed. The one vulnerability they really have is the wire itself; if 
it’s cut, the connection is broken. That means, when you’re laying out 
wires, you need to consider the best way to protect them from damage. 
In war movies  you’ll often see  field telephone links  being  knocked out  
by artillery fire cutting the wires. This can happen, but in reality the  
biggest threat to the wire is vehicles. Tracked combat vehicles are the  
worst – the wire often gets tangled in the track links, and the end result  
is usually hundreds of feet of wire being uprooted before it finally snags  
on something and breaks. Wheeled vehicles can also do a lot of damage,  
though. Just running a wheel over a wire on a rough, hard surface can  
shred the insulation and weaken or kill the signal. It’s best to put wires  
where there’s no chance of anyone driving into or over them. 
An obvious place to string the wire is between existing telephone poles.  
There’s no need to bother with the insulators used for regular phone  
wires – just use a staple or cable tie to fix them in place. If you want to 
conceal the wire, fix it to the cables that are already up there. They’ll  
be dead, so there won’t be any interference, and a thin, black field  
phone line will be almost invisible up there. 
You can also run the wire between trees, high enough that anyone  
walking or driving between the trees won’t snag it. The foliage will also  
help hire it. Just remember to string the wire loose enough that it won’t  
break if the trees sway in a high wind. If it doesn’t have to cross any  
roads it can also be fastened to walls, fences and other barriers; that  
will both protect and conceal it. 
The main reason to conceal the wire is to stop anyone damaging it.  
Anyone who’s might be planning to attack you have a reason to knock 
out your phones, but there’s also a risk from people who weren’t  
prepared for the crisis, and resent those who were. If they’re bitter  
enough, they might just tear your wires down to make your life worse.

A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
Field telephones are very secure; the only way to intercept the signal  
is to physically attach an intercept device to the wire. They also can’t  
be jammed. The one vulnerability they really have is the wire itself; if 
it’s cut, the connection is broken. That means, when you’re laying out 
wires, you need to consider the best way to protect them from damage. 
In war movies  you’ll often see  field telephone links  being  knocked out  
by artillery fire cutting the wires. This can happen, but in reality the  
biggest threat to the wire is vehicles. Tracked combat vehicles are the  
worst – the wire often gets tangled in the track links, and the end result  
is usually hundreds of feet of wire being uprooted before it finally snags  
on something and breaks. Wheeled vehicles can also do a lot of damage,  
though. Just running a wheel over a wire on a rough, hard surface can  
shred the insulation and weaken or kill the signal. It’s best to put wires  
where there’s no chance of anyone driving into or over them. 
An obvious place to string the wire is between existing telephone poles.  
There’s no need to bother with the insulators used for regular phone  
wires – just use a staple or cable tie to fix them in place. If you want to 
conceal the wire, fix it to the cables that are already up there. They’ll  
be dead, so there won’t be any interference, and a thin, black field  
phone line will be almost invisible up there. 
You can also run the wire between trees, high enough that anyone  
walking or driving between the trees won’t snag it. The foliage will also  
help hire it. Just remember to string the wire loose enough that it won’t  
break if the trees sway in a high wind. If it doesn’t have to cross any  
roads it can also be fastened to walls, fences and other barriers; that  
will both protect and conceal it. 
The main reason to conceal the wire is to stop anyone damaging it.  
Anyone who’s might be planning to attack you have a reason to knock 
out your phones, but there’s also a risk from people who weren’t  
prepared for the crisis, and resent those who were. If they’re bitter  
enough, they might just tear your wires down to make your life worse.

40 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
shovel. Feed the wire into the slit and stamp it down lightly – not hard 
enough to leave marks. As long as the wire’s insulation is in good shape  
it will work fine, even if the ground is wet. 
Field telephones are more secure than radios, but they’re not totally  
impossible to intercept. If someone can splice their own wire into yours,  
they can attach a phone to the end of it and listen in. If your wires  
aren’t all inside the area that you can effectively observe and secure,  
and you have something important to say, you can use any of the  
methods that work for secure radio messages. 
Secret writing 
There might be times when you need to put something in writing, but 
you don’t want it to be read. Say you need to get a message to someone 
who doesn’t have a radio; you might need to write them a letter and  
give it to someone to pass on to them. The question is, how much do  
you trust the person you’re giving the letter to? Unless you’re 
completely sure, it might be a good idea to make sure they can read it 
without knowing what it really says. 
One simple way to do this is to write in invisible ink. It’s an ancient  
method, but still a very effective one. What you do is write a convincing,  
but harmless, letter that doesn’t reveal anything important. Then you 
use the remaining space on the page to write another, secret, message 
that won’t show up unless someone knows how to reveal it. 
Modern invisible ink usually glows under an ultraviolet light, but most 
people don’t have an ultraviolet light handy. You probably don’t keep 
too many invisible ink pens around the house, either (although you  
should – they’re a good way to mark anything that might be attractive 
to thieves). Luckily there are older ways to make invisible ink, and they  
still work very well. 
Centuries ago a solution of ferrous sulfate was used as an invisible ink. 
A message could be written with it, and would disappear completely

source_components.text:
41 
A Spec Ops Untraceable Communication Guide 
when dry. However, when the paper was heated the message would  
reappear. If you don’t have any ferrous sulfate handy you can get  
exactly the same effect with lemon juice. The only problem with that is 
that the letter will smell of lemons for a while after the message is  
written, and someone might guess what you’ve done. If you can, leave 
it for a while to let the smell fade before you put it in an envelope and 
send it. 
Messages written with these inks don’t need a lot of heat to reveal  
them. There’s no danger of the hidden writing appearing from 
someone’s body heat, but you don’t need to risk setting fire to them  
either. Holding it close to a light bulb will usually be enough. 
There’s another way to hide a message in a letter without using 
invisible ink, but it needs a bit more preparation and you have to use  
some artistry to pull it off, but if it works it’s very effective. It’s called  
a mask letter. 
To write a mask letter you need a mask – a sheet of paper the same  
size as your notepaper, with blocks cut out of it in a random pattern.  
To write a message, you put the mask on top of a sheet of paper and  
write the message in the blocks. Then you take the mask off and  
compose a normal, innocent letter around the secret one. When the  
letter gets to the other end, all the receiver has to do is put their own  
mask over it and the hidden message will appear. 
Obviously there’s a potential weakness here – sender and receiver both  
need to have a copy of the mask. This isn’t a method you can use  
without preparing in advance. If you have prepared however, it’s very 
effective. Cops and anyone who knows something about secret writing 
will routinely heat up any letters they’re suspicious of, just to see if  
invisible ink has been used. They might also use UV and chemicals. A  
well-written mask letter, however, is immune to all of these tricks.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
7 
Chapter 1: The First 48 Hours 
Most people lose the first 48 hours to shock. They sit, they watch, they wait to see if things 
calm down. By the time they accept that things are not calming down, the water has 
stopped running, the shops have been emptied, and the window for leaving safel y has 
already started to close. 
Do not lose those hours. Here is how to use them. 
Accept it is real before you feel ready to 
The hardest thing in the first hours is not logistics. It is getting your brain to stop looking 
for the version of events where everything goes back to normal by Tuesday. That version 
does not exist. The sooner you let go of it, the sooner you can actually help your family. 
You do not need certainty to act. You need enough information to know that waiting is 
worse than moving. If explosions are close, if armed groups are on your streets, if shops 
are shutting and neighbors are boarding windows, that is enough. Stop waiting for official 
confirmation. In a collapse, official confirmation comes late, or not at all. 
Fill every container with water. Right now. 
The first time I told someone to do this, they thought I was being dramatic. In our city, tap 
water stopped within four days of the fighting reaching our neighborhood. Four days 
sounds like enough time until you are living through it. 
Fill your bathtub. Fill your pots, your bottles, your buckets. Do it before anything else 
because once the pressure drops it does not come back. This single action has more 
practical impact on your first week of survival than almost anything else you will do in 
these 48 hours. 
Count your food honestly 
Do not cook a big meal to use things up. Do not think about what might spoil. Sit down 
and count: how many days can you feed your family on what is in your kitchen right now, 
eating less than normal? Write that number down. It is one of the most important 
numbers you will have, and knowing it prevents panic-driven decisions later.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
9 
What you should have by hour 48 
Water stockpiled for at least a week. A food count and a rough rationing plan. Two or three 
neighbors you are in basic communication with. A working radio or reliable information 
source. A charged phone with numbers saved offline.  
And either a decision to stay, or a bag packed with documents, medicine, cash, and warm 
layers, ready to move. 
That bag should have been packed before you needed it. Pack it now anyway.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
12 
This does not mean you should isolate yourself. It means that if a building you are in 
becomes conspicuously full and conspicuously active, that is a reason to think about 
whether it is still the right place to be. 
5. You have already heard it discussed 
This one sounds almost too simple, but it saved us once. 
Information moves through a war zone in strange ways. You will overhear things. 
Someone on the street will say something to someone else. A name or an address will 
come up in conversation in a way that has a particular weight to it.  
People will refer to a location using language that signals it is contested, watched, or 
already marked. 
If you hear a specific building mentioned more than once in contexts that feel loaded, 
take that seriously. In our neighborhood, I heard our local police post mentioned twice in 
two days by people speaking in lowered voices.  
Two days later it was raided. I do not know exactly what those people knew or how they 
knew it. But they knew something, and the fact that they were talking about it, even 
obliquely, was the signal. 
Listen to what people around you are saying. Not to gather intelligence in any formal 
sense, just to notice which places are being named and how. In a war, the places nobody 
wants to talk about directly are often the places something is about to happen. 
A note on timing 
Recognizing these signs is only useful if you act on them fast enough. The instinct is to 
wait and see, to not overreact, to not drag your family out of a relatively stable shelter on 
a hunch. That instinct will cost you. 
When you see two or more of these signs in the same building or area, start moving. You 
do not need all five. You do not need certainty. The cost of leaving a building unnecessarily 
is inconvenience. The cost of staying in one that gets hit is everything. 
Move first. Reassess once you are clear.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
14 
- Where are the tall or elevated structures? What do they overlook? 
- Are there long straight stretches where you would be exposed for more than a few 
seconds? 
- Are there intersections with no cover on approach? 
- Are there windows or rooftops you cannot see into clearly? 
- Is there debris, sandbag placement, or damage that suggests a position has 
already been used? 
Sandbags are an obvious sign. But also look for subtler things: fabric or dark material 
hung inside a window to reduce visibility from outside, a cleared space on a rooftop 
where rubble has been moved, scorch marks or impact patterns on walls that indicate a 
previous exchange of fire, which tells you a contested zone exists there. 
The specific terrain features that kill people 
After years of moving through a city at war, certain patterns become clear. These are the 
situations that account for most sniper casualties among civilians: 
Intersections. Crossing an intersection means stepping into open ground with exposure 
on multiple axes. If a position exists at the far end of either street, you are visible for the 
entire crossing. Never walk casually through an intersection in a contested area. Move 
fast, use whatever cover exists on the near side first, and cross one person at a time if you 
are in a group. 
Open ground between buildings.  Gaps between structures, empty lots, collapsed 
sections that create a clear line of sight across a block. These feel less dangerous than 
intersections because they are not road crossings, but they can be just as exposed. Map 
them in your head and find ways around them. 
Ground floor windows facing long streets. If you are inside a building, do not sit or stand 
near a window that faces a long straight street. You are visible from further away than you 
think, especially if you are backlit by a light source inside. 
Predictable routes. If you walk the same path at the same time every day, a patient 
shooter eventually has all the information they need. Vary your timing, vary your route 
where possible, and avoid becoming a pattern. 
Moving through a dangerous area 
When you have no choice but to move through terrain you cannot fully read, these are the 
principles that keep you alive:

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
14 
- Where are the tall or elevated structures? What do they overlook? 
- Are there long straight stretches where you would be exposed for more than a few 
seconds? 
- Are there intersections with no cover on approach? 
- Are there windows or rooftops you cannot see into clearly? 
- Is there debris, sandbag placement, or damage that suggests a position has 
already been used? 
Sandbags are an obvious sign. But also look for subtler things: fabric or dark material 
hung inside a window to reduce visibility from outside, a cleared space on a rooftop 
where rubble has been moved, scorch marks or impact patterns on walls that indicate a 
previous exchange of fire, which tells you a contested zone exists there. 
The specific terrain features that kill people 
After years of moving through a city at war, certain patterns become clear. These are the 
situations that account for most sniper casualties among civilians: 
Intersections. Crossing an intersection means stepping into open ground with exposure 
on multiple axes. If a position exists at the far end of either street, you are visible for the 
entire crossing. Never walk casually through an intersection in a contested area. Move 
fast, use whatever cover exists on the near side first, and cross one person at a time if you 
are in a group. 
Open ground between buildings.  Gaps between structures, empty lots, collapsed 
sections that create a clear line of sight across a block. These feel less dangerous than 
intersections because they are not road crossings, but they can be just as exposed. Map 
them in your head and find ways around them. 
Ground floor windows facing long streets. If you are inside a building, do not sit or stand 
near a window that faces a long straight street. You are visible from further away than you 
think, especially if you are backlit by a light source inside. 
Predictable routes. If you walk the same path at the same time every day, a patient 
shooter eventually has all the information they need. Vary your timing, vary your route 
where possible, and avoid becoming a pattern. 
Moving through a dangerous area 
When you have no choice but to move through terrain you cannot fully read, these are the 
principles that keep you alive:

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
15 
- Hug walls rather than walking down the center of a street. The angle of exposure 
from an elevated position is much narrower close to a building. 
- Move in short bursts between points of cover rather than walking continuously in 
the open. Identify your next covered position before you leave your current one. 
- Cross open ground quickly and without hesitation. Stopping in the middle of an 
exposed stretch to look around is the worst thing you can do. 
- If you are moving as a family or group, do not bunch together. Space yourselves 
out. It is harder to watch and it means a single shot does not affect everyone. 
- Trust the locals. If the people who live in a neighborhood are consistently avoiding 
a certain street or crossing, there is a reason. Ask, or simply follow their lead. 
Signs a position is actively occupied 
There is a difference between terrain that could support a sniper and terrain that currently 
does. These are the indicators that suggest active occupation: 
- Civilian avoidance. If an area that should have foot traffic is empty, and the few people 
you see are moving fast and close to walls, treat it as confirmed dangerous. 
- Recent impact marks on walls at roughly human height, which indicate aimed fire rather 
than indiscriminate shelling. 
- The sound of a single shot rather than sustained fire. Snipers do not spray. One shot, 
then silence, is a specific signature. 
- Animals behaving unusually. This sounds like folklore but it is not. Dogs and cats in a 
neighborhood learn the dangerous zones faster than people do. An area that has strays 
but no animals is worth noticing. 
When you get it wrong 
You will not always read the terrain correctly. Nobody does. The goal is not perfect threat 
detection, it is reducing your exposure enough that mistakes are survivable. 
If you find yourself in the open and uncertain, do not freeze. Move to the nearest cover 
immediately, even if it is imperfect. A parked car, a doorway, a low wall. Crouching behind 
something imperfect is better than standing in the open while you decide what to do. 
Once you are behind cover, take a breath and assess. Look at where other people are, 
what they are doing, which directions they are avoiding. Let the environment give you 
information before you move again.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
17 
Chapter 4: 7 Routes to Avoid When Moving 
Through Hostile Territory 
In the early months, before we understood how the city had reorganized itself, we moved 
around mostly on instinct and luck. That is a terrible system. We lost a neighbor to it. He 
took a road he had driven a thousand times before the war, a road that felt familiar and 
therefore felt safe. Familiar and safe are not the same thing anymore. They stop being the 
same thing the moment the war arrives. 
What follows is not a list of specific streets. It is a framework for identifying which routes 
in your city have become dangerous, so you can build your own mental map and keep it 
updated as things change. 
1. Roads that run parallel to front lines 
Front lines in urban warfare are rarely clean. They shift, they blur, they exist as contested 
blocks rather than drawn boundaries. But wherever two opposing forces are in proximity, 
the roads that run alongside that zone become extremely dangerous. 
These streets get used for fast vehicle movement by both sides. They attract fire from 
multiple directions. And because they sit between two forces rather than behind either 
one, they have no safe side. You are exposed regardless of which way you are facing. 
If you know or suspect where the nearest front line is, avoid any road that runs parallel to 
it within several blocks. Routes that cross perpendicular to a front line, moving you away 
from it, are generally safer than ones that keep you running alongside it. 
2. Main arterial roads and boulevards 
Before the war, these were the roads everyone used. Wide lanes, good visibility, fast 
movement. Every one of those qualities makes them dangerous now. 
Wide roads mean long exposure when crossing or traveling along them. Good visibility 
means anyone watching from an elevated position can see you clearly and from a 
distance.  
Fast vehicle movement means checkpoints get placed on them, which means armed 
men making fast decisions about who you are and why you are there.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
19 
5. Roads that pass through market areas or gathering 
points 
This one surprised people who had not thought it through. Markets, water distribution 
points, bread lines, and anywhere else civilians gather in numbers become targets for 
two reasons. 
First, they are visible concentrations of people, which makes them attractive targets for 
forces trying to create panic or assert control. 
 Second, they attract checkpoints, because controlling access to food and water is a form 
of power. Either way, the roads leading in and out of these areas see disproportionate 
incident rates, especially during periods of active fighting. 
If you need to use a market or distribution point, approach and leave by different routes 
each time. Do not linger on the approach roads. Get in, get what you need, and leave by 
a route you have not used before that day. 
6. Roads you have not personally verified recently 
A road that was safe three days ago may not be safe today. Checkpoints appear overnight. 
Rubble from a strike can change which routes are passable. A building collapse can 
funnel everyone onto a single road, which then becomes predictable and watched. 
Do not rely on information that is more than 24 to 48 hours old for active route planning. 
Before using any route, try to verify it with someone who has used it that day, or who lives 
along it and can tell you what the current situation is. 
The most reliable sources are: 
- Neighbors or contacts who moved through that area that morning 
- Shopkeepers or residents along the route who are still present and operating 
- The behavior of other civilians, specifically whether they are using that road at all 
If a road that normally has foot traffic is empty, that emptiness is information. Treat it as 
such. 
7. The route everyone is using 
When a conflict settles into patterns, civilians develop shared routes. Word spreads that 
a particular road is currently safe and people converge on it. For a while, they are right. 
The road is relatively safe.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
20 
Then it becomes predictable. And predictable routes in a war get watched, get targeted, 
or get checkpointed by whoever wants to control movement in that area. The very fact 
that everyone is using a road is eventually a reason to stop using it. 
This does not mean you should take unnecessary risks trying to find obscure alternatives. 
It means you should be paying attention to when a shared route starts feeling too 
established, too routine, too known. When you start to feel like a pattern, it is ti me to 
change the pattern. 
Building and maintaining your mental map 
None of this is useful as abstract knowledge. It has to become a living map in your head, 
one you are constantly updating. 
Every time you move through the city, you are gathering information. Note what you see: 
where vehicles are positioned, which roads have fresh impact damage, where crowds are 
forming, which routes locals are avoiding. When you get home, share that informati on 
with whoever you trust. When they go out, ask them what they saw. 
Over time this builds into something genuinely valuable: a picture of how your city is 
organized right now, not how it was before the war. That picture will be out of date by 
tomorrow, which is why you keep updating it. 
The people who moved most safely through our city were not the bravest or the fastest. 
They were the ones who treated movement as information-gathering, who never stopped 
paying attention, and who were willing to turn around and go home when something felt  
wrong. 
That last part matters. Turning around is not weakness. It is the correct decision more 
often than you would expect. Go home, wait, gather more information, and try again 
tomorrow. Tomorrow you might know something you do not know today.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
21 
Chapter 5: How to Navigate Checkpoints 
Without Getting Detained 
I was stopped at checkpoints hundreds of times over seven years. Most were routine. A 
few were not. The difference between the two was rarely about luck.  
It was almost always about preparation, behavior, and understanding what the person on 
the other side of that barrier actually wanted from the interaction. 
A checkpoint is not a trial. It is not an interrogation, most of the time. It is a control 
mechanism staffed by people who are tired, often frightened, sometimes poorly trained, 
and trying to make fast decisions about strangers.  
Your job is to make that decision as easy as possible for them. You want to be the most 
boring person they see all day. 
What checkpoints are actually for 
Understanding the purpose of a checkpoint changes how you approach it. 
Depending on who is running it, a checkpoint is trying to do one or more of the following: 
• Screen for fighters or people affiliated with the opposing side 
• Control the movement of weapons, ammunition, or supplies 
• Extract money, goods, or information from civilians passing through 
• Assert territorial control and visibility over who is moving in and out 
• Gather intelligence on what is happening in areas they do not control 
Most of the time, with most checkpoints, they are not looking for you specifically. They 
are running a filter, and you want to pass through that filter without catching on anything. 
The ones that are actively looking for someone specific are the dangerous ones, and there 
is a separate section on those below. 
Before you reach the checkpoint 
The work happens before you get there, not at the barrier itself. 
Know who is running it.  Whenever possible, find out in advance whose checkpoint you 
are approaching. Government forces, opposition groups, and local militias each have

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
22 
different priorities and different things that will flag you as a problem. A document that 
reassures one group may be the wrong thing to show another. Ask people who have 
passed through recently. This is one of the most valuable pieces of information your 
neighborhood network can provide. 
Have your documents ready but not in your hand. You want to be able to produce them 
quickly and calmly, not be fumbling through a bag while a soldier watches you. Know 
exactly where they are. At the same time, do not walk up to a checkpoint already holding 
your papers out. That can read as nervous or rehearsed. 
Have a clear, simple, consistent story.  Where are you coming from? Where are you 
going? Why? The answers should be short, truthful where possible, and free of details 
that invite follow -up questions. The more you say, the more there is to probe. Practice 
your answer before you get there, not be cause you are lying, but because clarity under 
stress requires preparation. 
Remove anything that could be misread. Before approaching a checkpoint, think about 
what you are carrying. Certain equipment, certain books, certain clothing can flag you as 
a problem depending on who is asking. Think about this in advance, not at the barrier. 
At the barrier 
Your behavior in the first thirty seconds sets the tone for the entire interaction. 
• Slow down well before the checkpoint. Approaching too fast, even in a vehicle, 
signals either aggression or panic. Come in slowly and stop where they indicate 
without being told twice. 
• Keep your hands visible at all times.  In a vehicle, hands on the wheel. On foot, 
hands relaxed at your sides or in front of you. Do not reach into pockets or bags 
without being asked and without narrating what you are doing. "I am getting my 
identification" before you reach for it. 
• Make eye contact but do not stare.  You want to appear calm and cooperative, 
not challenging. Look at the person speaking to you. Do not look around at the 
other soldiers, the weapons, or the surroundings. Looking around reads as 
surveillance. 
• Do not smile too much. This sounds strange but excessive friendliness reads as 
performance. Be polite, be calm, be neutral. You are not trying to charm them. You 
are trying to be unremarkable. 
• Answer what is asked. Nothing more.  Do not volunteer information. Do not 
explain things that were not questioned. Do not fill silences with more talking. 
Silence is uncomfortable for you and normal for them. Let them break it.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
23 
Documents and what to carry 
In a civil war, the document landscape shifts constantly. What is valid, what is required, 
and what is suspicious changes depending on who controls the area and how the conflict 
is evolving. That said, some general principles hold: 
• Carry original documents, not copies where possible. Copies invite questions 
about where the originals are. 
• Carry documents for every person in your group, including children. A family with 
papers for the adults but not the children creates questions. 
• If you have work documents that establish a legitimate reason for movement, 
such as something connecting you to medical work, humanitarian activity, or 
essential services, carry them. These categories receive different treatment at 
most checkpoints. 
• Do not carry documents or materials that associate you with any political or 
armed group unless you are specifically passing through a checkpoint run by that 
group and the association is an asset. 
• Keep documents in a consistent, accessible place every single time. The habit 
matters. 
When the interaction becomes difficult 
Sometimes, despite doing everything right, the interaction turns. The soldier is having a 
bad day. Someone in your group resembles a description they have been given. They 
decide they want to search your vehicle or your bags. 
If this happens: 
• Stay calm. Your visible stress makes their suspicion worse. 
• Cooperate with the search fully and without protest. Objecting to a search at a 
checkpoint run by armed men is almost never the right decision. 
• Do not make jokes. Do not be sarcastic. Do not reference laws or rights. None of 
that framework applies here. 
• If they are asking questions you genuinely do not know the answer to, say so 
simply. "I don't know" is a better answer than a guess that unravels. 
• If they are detaining you or separating you from your group, do not resist physically. 
Your goal at that moment is to stay calm, stay communicative, and give them no 
additional reason to escalate. Escalation is almost never in your favor.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
23 
Documents and what to carry 
In a civil war, the document landscape shifts constantly. What is valid, what is required, 
and what is suspicious changes depending on who controls the area and how the conflict 
is evolving. That said, some general principles hold: 
• Carry original documents, not copies where possible. Copies invite questions 
about where the originals are. 
• Carry documents for every person in your group, including children. A family with 
papers for the adults but not the children creates questions. 
• If you have work documents that establish a legitimate reason for movement, 
such as something connecting you to medical work, humanitarian activity, or 
essential services, carry them. These categories receive different treatment at 
most checkpoints. 
• Do not carry documents or materials that associate you with any political or 
armed group unless you are specifically passing through a checkpoint run by that 
group and the association is an asset. 
• Keep documents in a consistent, accessible place every single time. The habit 
matters. 
When the interaction becomes difficult 
Sometimes, despite doing everything right, the interaction turns. The soldier is having a 
bad day. Someone in your group resembles a description they have been given. They 
decide they want to search your vehicle or your bags. 
If this happens: 
• Stay calm. Your visible stress makes their suspicion worse. 
• Cooperate with the search fully and without protest. Objecting to a search at a 
checkpoint run by armed men is almost never the right decision. 
• Do not make jokes. Do not be sarcastic. Do not reference laws or rights. None of 
that framework applies here. 
• If they are asking questions you genuinely do not know the answer to, say so 
simply. "I don't know" is a better answer than a guess that unravels. 
• If they are detaining you or separating you from your group, do not resist physically. 
Your goal at that moment is to stay calm, stay communicative, and give them no 
additional reason to escalate. Escalation is almost never in your favor.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
24 
The checkpoints that are actually looking for you 
If your name is on a list, if you have been identified as affiliated with the opposing side, if 
someone has informed on you, then a checkpoint stops being a filter and becomes a trap. 
These situations are different and require different thinking. 
The best defense against this scenario is avoiding checkpoints where this risk exists. If 
you have any reason to believe your name or identity is flagged with a particular force, do 
not pass through their checkpoints if there is any alternative. This is no t cowardice. It is 
the correct calculation. 
If you are in a situation where you cannot avoid it, the calculus changes entirely and 
depends heavily on specifics that no general guide can fully address. What matters most 
in that situation is prior intelligence, knowing as precisely as possible what they have and 
what they are looking for, so you can make an informed decision about whether to 
attempt the crossing at all. 
After you are through 
Once you are past a checkpoint, keep moving at a normal pace for at least a block before 
doing anything else. Do not stop immediately to check your phone, adjust your bags, or 
express relief. You may still be visible and you want to remain unremarkable until you are 
genuinely clear. 
Note the checkpoint's location, who was running it, what they asked, and how the 
interaction felt. Share that information with anyone in your network who may need to use 
that route. Every piece of current intelligence about checkpoint behavior is valuable to 
someone. 
The goal every time is the same: be the most forgettable person they processed that day. 
Arrive calm, answer simply, leave cleanly. Most of the time, if you have prepared properly, 
that is exactly what happens.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
26 
The politics of survival: say nothing, commit to 
nothing 
The single most protective thing you can do politically is to be aggressively neutral. 
Do not display symbols, flags, or slogans associated with either side in or around your 
home. Do not sign petitions, attend rallies, or participate in any organized activity that 
could be recorded and used to establish your affiliation. Do not have those conversations 
with people you do not completely trust, and be very careful about how completely you 
trust anyone during a civil war. 
When asked directly about your political sympathies, which will happen at checkpoints, 
during raids, and in casual conversation with armed men, have a rehearsed answer that 
is warm, vague, and commits to nothing. Express concern for your family. Express 
exhaustion with the violence. Express a desire for peace. None of these things identify 
you as belonging to either camp. All of them are true. 
This is not cowardice. This is the correct strategy for keeping your family alive when both 
sides are dangerous. There will be time for politics after the war. During it, politics is a 
liability. 
Managing your household's visibility 
Both sides are looking for information about the areas they operate in. The less your 
household stands out, the less information there is to gather about you. 
• Keep the exterior of your home as neutral and unremarkable as possible. Visible 
wealth invites looting. Visible damage invites assumptions about what happened 
there. 
• Limit who knows the details of your household. How many people live there, 
whether there are men of fighting age, whether you have supplies stockpiled. This 
information travels. 
• Be consistent in your routines enough to appear normal, but not so consistent that 
your patterns become predictable to someone watching. 
• If armed men occupy a building near you or move into your street, do not watch 
them. Do not photograph them. Do not discuss them loudly. You are not there to 
observe them and they should not feel observed.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
27 
potential insurgents or conscripts. Armed groups will see them as potential recruits or, if 
they have refused to join, as suspicious. 
There is no single answer to managing this risk. In some situations, having 
documentation that ties a man to an essential civilian role, medical worker, engineer, 
baker, provides some protection. In others, the documentation makes no difference to 
someone with a quota to fill. 
What matters most is awareness. Men of fighting age should not be the ones answering 
the door during raids or moving through high-risk areas without clear purpose.  
They should have a cover story for their non-participation that is plausible and consistent. 
And the household should have a plan for what happens if they are detained, because 
the possibility should be planned for, not ignored. 
When one side comes to your door 
This will happen. It may happen more than once. The principles are consistent regardless 
of which side is knocking. 
Open the door. Do not make them break it down. The act of opening the door signals 
cooperation and reduces the chance of an aggressive entry that is dangerous to everyone 
inside. 
Be calm and defer immediately. You are not negotiating. You are not defending your rights. 
You are a cooperative civilian with nothing to hide and nowhere urgent to be. Answer 
questions simply, offer nothing extra, and keep your family calm and visible behind you. 
If they want to search, let them search. Move through the home with them if they allow it, 
not to supervise them but to maintain a calm presence and reduce the chance of things 
escalating due to a family member reacting badly. 
If they take things, let them take things. Possessions can be replaced or survived without. 
A confrontation over possessions can end in ways that cannot be recovered from. 
If they want to take a person, that is a different situation. Stay calm, ask where they are 
being taken, try to get a name and unit if possible. Do not physically resist.  
The goal from that point is to know where your person is so you can work to get them back, 
and that process starts with information, not confrontation.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
28 
Playing both sides without being caught 
In some situations, survival requires performing loyalty to whoever is in front of you at that 
moment. This is not collaboration. It is theater, and almost everyone in a long civil war 
ends up doing some version of it. 
The risk is being caught performing it for the other side. People talk. Informants exist on 
both sides. If you have been seen cooperating warmly with government forces, and then 
the area changes hands and an opposition group arrives, that history can be used against 
you. 
Manage this by keeping your performances of loyalty as minimal as possible. Cooperate, 
defer, answer questions, but do not volunteer enthusiasm.  
Do not become the person who went out of their way to help one side, because that story 
will follow you. The goal is to be remembered as compliant and unremarkable, not as an 
ally. 
The hardest part 
There will come a point where protecting your family's neutrality costs you something. A 
neighbor who needs help and whose political affiliations are dangerous to be associated 
with. A family member who wants to take a side and fight. A situation where speaking up 
is the right thing and the wrong thing at the same time. 
I cannot tell you what to do in those moments. No guide can. What I can tell you is that 
the families who survived intact were almost always the ones who kept the circle tight. 
Immediate family first.  
Neutrality as a discipline, not just a preference. Every exception to that rule was a risk, 
and some of those risks did not end well. 
That is the brutal arithmetic of a civil war. You protect what you can protect. You accept 
that you cannot protect everything.  
And you make peace, as best you can, with the distance between those two things.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
31 
People who are already helping others quietly.  Not loudly, not publicly, but who you 
discover through indirect means are providing small forms of assistance to people 
around them. This behavior is a reliable indicator of character and of the kind of person 
who understands how mutual support works. 
People with complementary skills or resources.  A network where everyone has the 
same skills is less valuable than one where different people can provide different things. 
Someone with medical knowledge. Someone with a vehicle. Someone with connections 
outside the neighborhood. Someone who is good at g etting information. Diversity of 
capability is the point. 
People who do not talk too much. In a war, the people who share everything they know 
with everyone they meet are liabilities regardless of their intentions. The people who are 
naturally discreet, who you notice do not repeat things unnecessarily, are safer to have 
inside a network. 
People with a consistent track record under pressure. How did they behave during the 
hardest recent period? Did they share resources when it cost them something? Did they 
stay when others fled? Did they keep their word in circumstances where breaking it would 
have been easy? Past behavior under stress is the  best available predictor of future 
behavior under stress. 
How to build the relationship slowly 
You do not recruit someone into your network. You develop a relationship incrementally, 
testing at each stage before going deeper. 
The process roughly follows this pattern: 
Start with small practical exchanges. Help with something that costs you little and 
observe how it is received and reciprocated. Lend a tool. Share information about a 
checkpoint that is useful but not sensitive. Help carry something heavy. These 
interactions establish goodwill and give you early data about how the person behaves. 
Progress to slightly more meaningful exchanges. Share a piece of information that is more 
current or more specific. Ask for help with something that requires a small amount of 
effort on their part.  
Note whether they follow through, whether they are discreet about it, whether they ask 
for anything in return and what. 
Only after this foundation exists should you begin to share anything sensitive or rely on 
them for anything critical. And even then, compartmentalize. No single person in your 
network needs to know everything about your situation.

source_components.text:
A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
32 
Different people know different things. This is not paranoia. It is basic operational sense. 
The informant problem 
Informants exist in every conflict and in every neighborhood. Some are ideologically 
motivated. Most are not. Most are people who are being coerced, compensated, or who 
have calculated that the cost of not cooperating is higher than the cost of cooperation. 
You will probably never know with certainty who the informants are. What you can do is 
structure your network so that a single informant cannot damage everything at once. 
Some practical principles: 
• Do not hold group meetings where sensitive information is discussed. The more 
people in a room, the higher the probability that someone in that room is 
compromised. 
• Separate your network into clusters that do not all know each other. If one cluster 
is penetrated, the others are not automatically exposed. 
• Pay attention to patterns. If sensitive information you shared with a specific 
person, and only that person, has a habit of reaching the wrong ears, that is data. 
It takes two or three instances to establish a pattern but once you see it, act on it 
immediately. 
• Do not confront someone you suspect. Remove them from your network quietly, 
stop sharing information with them, and let the relationship fade. Confrontation 
creates enemies. A quiet fade creates nothing. 
What to do when someone betrays you 
It will happen at some point. Not necessarily dramatically. More often it is a slow 
realization that someone you trusted made a calculation that did not include your 
wellbeing. 
When it happens, resist the impulse to shut everything down. One bad actor in a network 
does not mean the whole network is compromised, and the network is too valuable to 
abandon over a single failure. 
Contain the damage. Figure out what they knew and who they might have told it to. Adjust 
your behavior and your exposure accordingly. Then review your remaining relationships 
with fresh eyes, not with paranoia but with the updated information you now have about 
how people behave under pressure.

person, and only that person, has a habit of reaching the wrong ears, that is data. 
It takes two or three instances to establish a pattern but once you see it, act on it 
immediately. 
• Do not confront someone you suspect. Remove them from your network quietly, 
stop sharing information with them, and let the relationship fade. Confrontation 
creates enemies. A quiet fade creates nothing. 
What to do when someone betrays you 
It will happen at some point. Not necessarily dramatically. More often it is a slow 
realization that someone you trusted made a calculation that did not include your 
wellbeing. 
When it happens, resist the impulse to shut everything down. One bad actor in a network 
does not mean the whole network is compromised, and the network is too valuable to 
abandon over a single failure. 
Contain the damage. Figure out what they knew and who they might have told it to. Adjust 
your behavior and your exposure accordingly. Then review your remaining relationships 
with fresh eyes, not with paranoia but with the updated information you now have about 
how people behave under pressure.

A Syrian Survivor’s Civil War Guide 
33 
The goal is to learn from it without being destroyed by it. Every network that survives a 
long conflict has been through at least one betrayal. The ones that kept functioning were 
the ones that treated it as information rather than catastrophe. 
The thing networks are really for 
The practical benefits, the food, the information, the help with tasks, are real and 
important. But there is something else that a network provides that is harder to name and 
equally important. 
It provides the experience of not being entirely alone in what you are going through. 
Over seven years, the moments that came closest to breaking people were not always 
the most physically dangerous ones. They were the moments of complete isolation, 
when the weight of what was happening had no one to share it with, when the decisions 
were entirely yours and there was nobody to think alongside you. 
The people in our network kept each other sane in ways that had nothing to do with food 
or logistics. They remembered who we were before the war. They held that for each other. 
In a conflict that strips away most of what makes ordinary life feel worth living, that is not 
a small thing. 
Build the network for survival. Keep it for everything else too.
