A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
107 
Encourage the person to drink slowly and consistently. If they are 
unable to drink on their own, small amounts can be given carefully 
over time, as long as they are conscious and able to swallow safely. 
Watch for signs of worsening dehydration. These may include 
weakness, confusion, dry skin, reduced urination, or dizziness. If 
these signs appear, the situation is becoming more serious and 
requires immediate attention. 
Fluids alone may not resolve the underlying problem, but they play 
a critical role in keeping the body stable. 
In many cases, maintaining hydration can prevent a manageable 
condition from becoming life-threatening. 
Storage and Shelf Life 
Medicines are only useful if they remain effective. 
Store them in a cool, dry place, away from direct sunlight. Heat and 
moisture can reduce their effectiveness over time. 
Keep medications in their original packaging when possible. This 
helps you identify them and track expiration dates. 
While some medicines may remain usable past their listed date, you 
should always aim to keep your supply as fresh as possible. 
Organizing Your Supplies 
A well-organized medical supply is easier to use in an emergency. 
Keep similar items together and make sure you can find what you 
need quickly. In a stressful situation, you do not want to waste time 
searching. 
It is also helpful to keep your medical supplies in one place. This 
reduces confusion and makes it easier to restock when needed. 
Knowing What You Have 
Having medicine is not enough. You need to know what it is used 
for. 
Take time to understand the basic purpose of each item in your 
supply. This will help you make better decisions under pressure. 
If multiple people are involved, make sure others know where 
supplies are kept and how they are used.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
110 
Pain is a natural response to injury. 
In an emergency, it can become a serious problem. Severe pain 
makes it harder for a person to stay calm, follow instructions, or 
remain still. It can also increase stress on the body and make the 
situation worse. 
Managing pain is not just about comfort. It helps improve control, 
stability, and recovery. 
Why Pain Control Matters 
When pain is high, people tend to move more, panic, or make poor 
decisions. 
This can lead to: 
• worsening an injury 
• increased bleeding 
• higher stress on the body 
Reducing pain helps the person stay still and makes it easier to 
manage the situation. 
Even small improvements in comfort can have a big effect. 
Start with Stabilization 
The first step in reducing pain is not medication. It is stabilizing the 
injury. 
If a limb is injured, keep it still. Movement increases pain and can 
cause further damage. 
Support the injured area using whatever is available. This could be a 
splint, a piece of wood, or even firm fabric. The goal is to prevent 
movement as much as possible. 
For general injuries, have the person lie down or sit in a stable 
position. Avoid unnecessary movement. 
Use Positioning to Reduce Pain 
The way a person is positioned can make a difference. 
In many cases: 
• keeping the body supported reduces strain 
• elevating certain areas can reduce pressure 
• avoiding awkward positions helps prevent additional pain

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
111 
Let the person settle into a position that feels stable and reduces 
discomfort, as long as it does not interfere with safety. 
Apply Cold or Heat Carefully 
Cold can help reduce swelling and numb pain, especially in the early 
stages of an injury. 
A cold compress, wrapped in cloth, can be applied for short periods. 
Do not place ice directly on the skin. 
Heat can help with muscle tension or stiffness, but it should not be 
used on fresh injuries that involve swelling. 
Use these methods carefully and observe how the person responds. 
Using Basic Medications 
If available, basic over-the-counter medications can help manage 
pain. 
These can reduce discomfort and allow the person to rest. They can 
also help reduce inflammation in some cases. 
Use only what you understand and have used safely before. In a 
crisis, it is important not to create new risks. 
Managing Severe Pain with Limited 
Options 
In some situations, pain may be far more intense than simple 
methods can control. 
Severe injuries such as fractures, burns, or deep wounds can cause 
extreme discomfort. When pain reaches this level, it can interfere 
with breathing, movement, and the person’s ability to remain calm. 
In a setting without access to strong medication, your approach 
must rely on control rather than elimination of pain. 
The most effective method is still stabilization. 
Keeping the injured area completely still reduces the body’s 
response to pain. Even small movements can make the situation 
worse, so supporting the injury properly is essential. A well-placed 
splint or firm support can significantly reduce discomfort.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
112 
Pressure can also play a role. In some cases, steady pressure around 
an injury may reduce pain signals, particularly when swelling is 
present. This must be done carefully to avoid restricting circulation. 
Distraction and reassurance are more important than they may 
seem. A calm environment and clear communication help reduce 
anxiety, which in turn lowers the perception of pain. A person who 
feels in control will often tolerate pain better than one who is 
panicking. 
Cold can be used to reduce both swelling and pain in the early 
stages of an injury. Applied carefully and for short periods, it can 
provide noticeable relief. Heat may be useful later, once swelling has 
decreased, particularly for muscle tension. 
In extreme cases, when no other options are available, some people 
may consider the controlled use of alcohol to dull pain. This should 
be approached with caution. Alcohol can impair judgment, increase 
bleeding, and worsen the overall condition if used improperly. 
Pain cannot always be removed in an emergency. 
Your goal is to reduce it to a level that allows the person to remain 
still, think clearly, and cooperate with treatment. 
Even small improvements in comfort can have a meaningful impact 
on survival. 
Keeping the Person Calm 
Pain and stress are closely linked. 
A person who is anxious or afraid will often feel more pain. Keeping 
them calm can reduce how intense the pain feels. 
Speak clearly and calmly. Let them know what you are doing. Stay 
present and focused. 
A calm environment helps the body respond better. 
Avoid Making It Worse 
Some actions can increase pain or cause further injury. 
Avoid: 
• unnecessary movement 
• rough handling 
• forcing a position that causes discomfort

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
115 
In most emergencies, you focus on one person. 
In some situations, you may have to deal with several injured people 
at the same time. When that happens, you cannot treat everyone at 
once. 
You have to make decisions quickly about who needs help first. 
This is called triage. 
Understanding the Goal 
Triage is not about treating the worst-looking injury first. 
It is about treating the person who needs immediate help to survive. 
Some injuries may look serious but are stable. Others may not look 
severe but can become fatal within minutes. 
Your goal is to use your time where it will have the greatest impact. 
Three Simple Priority Levels 
You do not need a complex system. 
You can divide patients into three basic groups. 
First priority 
People who have life-threatening problems that can be treated right 
away. This includes severe bleeding or blocked breathing. These are 
the people you help first. 
Second priority 
People who are injured but stable. They may have broken bones or 
moderate wounds, but they are not in immediate danger. They can 
wait while you handle more urgent cases. 
Third priority 
People with minor injuries. They are conscious, able to move, and 
not at risk of immediate harm. These can wait the longest. 
This simple approach helps you stay focused. 
Quick Assessment 
When you arrive, move quickly from one person to the next. 
You are not doing full treatment yet. You are deciding priorities. 
Look for: 
• who is not responding 
• who is not breathing properly

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
116 
• who is bleeding heavily 
These are your first priority cases. 
Do not spend too much time on one person during this step. A few 
seconds per person is often enough to identify who needs help first. 
Start with What You Can Fix Fast 
Focus on problems you can improve quickly. 
Stopping severe bleeding or helping someone breathe can save a life 
in minutes. 
If someone has injuries that you cannot improve right away, you 
may need to move on and return later. 
This is one of the hardest parts of triage, but it is necessary when 
resources are limited. 
Keep People Where They Are 
Avoid moving injured people unless it is necessary for safety. 
Moving someone can make injuries worse, especially if you do not 
yet understand the full situation. 
Instead, move yourself between patients and provide care where 
they are. 
Reassess Regularly 
Triage is not done once. 
Conditions can change quickly. Someone who seemed stable may 
become worse, and someone treated earlier may improve. 
Go back and check on each person regularly. Adjust your priorities 
if needed. 
Staying in Control 
Managing multiple patients can feel overwhelming. 
Stay focused on one step at a time. Do not try to do everything at 
once. 
Work through your priorities. Handle the most urgent problem, 
then move to the next.

A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
119 
In a prolonged emergency, supplies do not last forever. 
Bandages run out. Disinfectants are used up. Access to proper 
equipment becomes limited or disappears completely. 
When that happens, you still need to act. Improvised care is not 
about perfect solutions. It is about using what you have in a way 
that is safe and effective. 
Think in Terms of Function 
When you do not have the right tools, focus on what the tool is 
supposed to do. 
A bandage is used to apply pressure and protect a wound. 
A splint is used to keep a limb from moving. 
Clean water is used to reduce contamination. 
If you understand the purpose, you can find alternatives. 
Do not focus on what is missing. Focus on what you need to 
achieve. 
Improvising Bandages and Dressings 
When medical bandages are not available, clean fabric becomes 
your best option. 
Clothing, towels, or sheets can be used if they are as clean as 
possible. Cut or tear them into usable pieces. 
The goal is to: 
• cover the wound 
• apply pressure if needed 
• protect it from further contamination 
If the material becomes soaked or dirty, replace it when possible. 
Creating Splints from Available 
Materials 
Stabilizing an injury is often more important than treating it. 
If you do not have a proper splint, use rigid objects to limit 
movement. Wood, sticks, boards, or even tightly rolled material can 
work.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
120 
Secure the splint using cloth, belts, or strips of fabric. It should be 
firm enough to prevent movement, but not so tight that it cuts off 
circulation. 
Always check that the area below the splint still has normal color 
and warmth. 
Basic Cleaning Without Medical 
Supplies 
Keeping wounds clean becomes more difficult when supplies are 
limited. 
If clean water is available, use it to rinse away dirt and debris. If 
water quality is uncertain, boiling it and letting it cool can make it 
safer. 
Avoid using dirty materials directly on open wounds. Even in a 
limited situation, taking a moment to improve cleanliness can 
reduce the risk of infection. 
Using Everyday Items Carefully 
Many everyday items can be useful in an emergency. 
A belt can help apply pressure or secure a splint. 
A piece of cloth can be folded to create padding. 
Containers can be used to store clean water for wound care. 
The key is to use items in a controlled and thoughtful way. Avoid 
anything that could introduce more harm than help. 
Managing Limited Resources 
When supplies are low, you must use them carefully. 
Do not use more than necessary. Save critical items for situations 
where they are truly needed. 
At the same time, do not hesitate to act when the situation is 
serious. Holding back when action is required can make things 
worse. 
Balance is important.

source_components.text:
A Combat Doctor’s SHTF Medicine Guide
122 
If tools must be used, they should be cleaned as thoroughly as 
possible. Boiling instruments in water for an extended period is one 
of the most reliable methods available in a limited setting. If this is 
not possible, using flame or alcohol can help reduce contamination, 
though these methods are less effective. 
Hands should be cleaned before and after any contact with the 
wound. The cleaner the environment, the lower the risk of 
infection. 
When dealing with a wound that cannot drain on its own, relieving 
pressure may become necessary. Swelling, trapped fluid, or infection 
beneath the surface can worsen over time if left untreated. In such 
cases, careful opening of the area may allow fluid to escape and 
reduce pressure. 
Bleeding must be controlled at all times. Even small amounts of 
uncontrolled bleeding can become dangerous without proper 
resources. Work slowly and apply pressure as needed. 
After any intervention, the wound should be cleaned and protected. 
Cover it with the cleanest material available and monitor it closely 
for signs of infection. 
Closure of a wound should only be considered if it has been 
properly cleaned. Sealing contamination inside the body can lead to 
serious complications. In some cases, it is safer to leave a wound 
open and continue cleaning it over time. 
Pain and stress will affect both the person being treated and the one 
providing care. Staying calm and working carefully will reduce the 
risk of mistakes. 
These situations are not ideal and should be avoided whenever 
possible. 
However, in a setting where no help is coming, careful action may 
provide a chance where there would otherwise be none.

10 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• The colors in nature are not all the same, and the colors you wear and 
that make up your gear and camp should also not be all the same. 
Choose several different colors that will effectively blend into your 
environment and paint your equipment with a disruptive pattern using 
fabric paint. 
• Know how the changing seasons affect the color scheme of the 
environment that you are operating in. Plan accordingly and choose 
camouflage patterns that will cover all the seasons or have a few sets of 
equipment and clothing so that you can effectively blend in despite the 
time of year. The difference may be negligible in arid regions, but the 
environment could change from lush green to brown and then white 
through the seasons in temperate areas. 
Shape  
Certain shapes either do not exist in nature or exist so rarely that they become 
immediately apparent.  
One such example is anything with a right angle, and another immediately 
apparent shape is the human form.  
In each of these cases, to effectively disappear, we need to transform these 
obvious outlines into something that looks natural.  
A few steps that we can take to counteract our shape from being our betrayer 
are:

15 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Shadow 
The problem with shadows is that when we hide behind an object, our shadow 
can be cast to the side, demonstrating to observers that someone is hiding 
there. However, using shadow to our advantage is possible and an essential 
aspect of becoming invisible in  the woods. In areas where there is a dark 
shadow cast, we can use these shadows to conceal ourselves further. This also 
applies to shadows cast by the moonlight as well. Even in the dark of night, 
there are areas that the light of the moon does not reach,  and these places can 
be fantastic places to find concealment. 
What we can do about the problem of shadows: 
• Make yourself aware of which direction the sun is shining and make sure 
that you will not cast a shadow in any direction that an observer may see. 
• If you are in an area for an extended period or are planning a permanent 
concealed position, keep a note of where shadows are cast and at which 
times. Use this knowledge to your advantage in planning the placement 
of your concealed positions. 
• Move from shadow to shadow and avoid the light at all costs when 
transiting areas. 
Silhouette  
Camouflage is effective as long as the background that we are blending into is 
similar to what we are wearing. If the sky is our background, then our disguise 
becomes useless.  
Avoiding silhouetting ourselves is something that the army drilled into us 
almost from day one. We can make few missteps regarding our camouflage that 
are as egregious and easily avoided as silhouetting ourselves. 
What we can do to avoid silhouetting ourselves:

source_components.text:
16 
16 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• Never walk along the top of a ridgeline. Instead, walk along the ridge at a 
point that is far enough below the crest where you will not find yourself 
silhouetted. Often this area is referred to as the military crest of a hill.  
• ALWAYS be aware of your background. Silhouetting does not always 
happen on a hilltop. If we walk within a treeline, the forest acts as an 
effective backdrop that conceals us, but the sky beyond the treeline 
serves to silhouette us to an observer within the forest. 
• If you must traverse a hill or ridge, either go around it or crawl over the 
top on your belly. 
Spacing  
Looking around any modern urban environment will show us that human 
beings like to space everything in an organized and even fashion. Nature, on the 
other hand, does not adhere to our need for organization. Much like shape, our 
eyes tend to be drawn to any spacing that looks artificial or 'man-made.' 
Fortunately, there are steps that we can take to avoid spacing being our 
downfall: 
• If you are placing several shelters in an area, randomize the spacing and 
orientation to avoid them catching the eye of someone observing the 
area. 
• The same is true for parking vehicles. Again, randomize the spacing and 
orientation of them to not look like a used car lot. 
Movement 
Most animals, humans included, are hardwired to detect movement. It is a 
survival instinct embedded into our DNA. But, unfortunately, even the best 
camouflage becomes useless if we move too much or at inopportune times.

17 
17 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• Use low ground (also referred to as 'dead ground') to conceal your 
movements. 
• Move under cover of darkness unless you are concerned about detection 
from thermal imaging or night vision. 
• Make all of your movements slow and deliberate avoid any sudden, 
violent, or jerky motions that may cause someone to take notice. 
Concluding Thoughts on ‘Why Things Are 
Seen’ 
To develop a good understanding of why things are seen, you must keep your 
eyes open to the world around you, noticing things that stand out and taking a 
second to think of why it is that you saw that object or person.  
If you want to be invisible in the outdoors, you need to begin by becoming very 
aware of your surroundings, and in turn, you will start to notice what is trying 
to avoid your detection.  
Being able to spot an animal, person, or object deliberately camouflaged is 
probably the most critical skill you should have to begin to make yourself 
invisible.

20 
20 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
be superior to no camouflage, there is no reason that you cannot operate 
invisibly in the outdoors wearing only earth-toned colors. 
The key to successfully blending into the environment without a camouflage 
pattern is to match the colors of your clothing to the colors of the environment 
you find yourself in. Earth tones are best, and they should be of fabrics that are 
either natural or appear natural.  
Camouflaging Your Skin 
No matter how great your clothing blends into the background, your skin will 
stand out. Even if your skin tone is dark, your skin will still be shiny, and your 
face still looks like a human face. Therefore, we need to apply face paint to your 
face to create a pattern that will disrupt the telltale features of the human face 
while eliminating the natural shine. 
Our goal in camouflaging the face is to transform it into something that no 
longer looks human -like. The best way to accomplish this is to lighten areas 
often in shadows, like the hollows of the eyes and the ears, then darken raised 
areas, such as our forehead, 
nose, and jawline. 
You will have to experiment 
a bit to match your face paint 
to your operating 
environment. That being 
said, regardless of what 
pattern you are going to 
apply to your face, the steps 
for using the paint will be the 
same.

23 
23 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
There are several styles and 
patterns that you will see 
soldiers and hunters use, but 
the truth is that as long as the 
face paint  makes your face 
look like anything other than 
a human face and blends well 
with the environment, your 
camouflage will be successful. 
Don't forget to either cover or 
camouflage your neck as well. 
Also, if you have a beard, you need to add some paint to your beard hair to help 
it blend into the rest of your face. 
If you do not have camouflage face paint, you can also use mud to smear your 
face to much the same effect. The only issue with this is that the mud will wash 
off far more readily than commercially bought camo face paint. 
Hands 
 1. Apply face paint on the backs of your hands 
as well.

26 
26 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
outline, less is more. There is no need to make ourselves look like a bush. We 
only need the shape of our body and equipment to appear no longer human -
like or artificial. 
Weapons And Gear 
The problem with firearms is, they have a distinct shape that looks like a 
firearm. They are also often manufactured in colors that stand out in the woods.  
Therefore, if you carry a gun with you as you disappear into the outdoors, paint 
it to blend in with your clothing and equipment's color scheme. Also, take 
measures to break up the weapon's outline to make it look less like a firearm.  
Painting a firearm can be done using readily available Earth tone spray paints 
with a flat finish. Several manufacturers of spray paint have product lines 
specifically for spray painting camouflage patterns. However, some paints are 
specifically designed for use on firearms, and these options usually require a lot 
more care and attention than spray paint. Of course, the trade -off is that the 
finish will last far longer. 
A few considerations that you need to take before painting a firearm will be: 
• Never paint internal components. These could become gummed up with 
paint causing malfunctions. 
• Use a variety of colors. 
• Always thoroughly clean and degrease the firearm before painting. 
• Mask any areas that you do not want to paint with painter's tape. 
• Wear a respirator and only paint in well-ventilated areas. 
• Use mesh, leaves, grass or other objects as stencils to create a unique 
camouflage pattern. 
• Use a light color as a base coat. Then, add the darker colors to create the 
pattern one at a time until you achieve the desired camouflage pattern. 
If you decide to paint your firearms, there are a few steps that you need to 
follow: 
1. Unload and clear the firearm. 
2. Disassemble the weapon and separate the parts you want to paint.

source_components.text:
27 
27 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
3. Clean the parts with a solvent and degreaser. Read and follow the 
manufacturer's instructions for the type of paint that you are using. In 
addition, there may be special cleaning and application instructions that 
you must follow. 
4. Prepare an area for painting, taking care to set up the space to eliminate 
the possibility of overspray getting on things that you don't want paint 
on. 
5. Wear the proper PPE and apply the first coat to the parts. Allow to dry 
and repeat the process until you are satisfied with the base coat. 
6. Use natural materials or mesh as a stencil and spray the next darker color. 
7. Repeat this process until you have sprayed all the colors you want on 
your weapon in the pattern you are happy with. 
8. Allow to dry and cure as per the manufacturer's directions. 
9. Reassemble the weapon, oil the internal components, and conduct a 
function test. 
Painting firearms will give you a massive advantage in your camouflage, but 
you can still up to your camo game by adding some materials such as pieces of 
a sniper's veil.  
The important thing to remember is that you do not want to add anything that 
will easily catch fire. The only places you should be placing additional 
camouflage are on the front handguard, the stock, and around the optics. 
Camouflaging Equipment 
Our equipment is also in need of camouflage. Fortunately, often we can 
purchase gear made from fabric that already has a camouflage pattern printed 
onto it. The problem is that all of this equipment still has a unique shape and 
could benefit from the addition of some natural camouflage. 
You could also tie or sew burlap strips to your gear, but this is not as effective 
as natural camouflage.

31 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Food that is lightweight, calorie -dense, and requires minimal preparation will 
help sustain your energy levels without slowing you down. 
Finally, you must carry a means of communication or signaling, whether it is a 
radio, whistle, or other method, to coordinate with others if necessary. 
These items form the foundation of your ability to survive and operate 
effectively. Everything else is secondary. If you are forced to make decisions 
about what to carry, these essentials should always take priority. 
Move Like A Ghost 
Knowing how things are seen and effectively camouflage ourselves is only the 
first few steps in becoming invisible in the outdoors. If you want to stay hidden, 
then you need to move through the woods like a ghost. The way we do this is to 
move quietly and to listen carefully. 
Footwork 
How we step is the first and most crucial part of becoming a ghost in the 
wilderness. Our feet are the parts of our body that constantly touch the ground 
and, with every step, threatening to give away our position. Of course, you can 
choose footwear like m occasins that are soft -soled and, in turn, very stealthy, 
but with proper technique, you can walk very quietly regardless of your 
footwear choices. The primary technique that we want to use when moving 
silently through the woods is 'Ghost Walking.' How it works is that as we step, 
the foot is set on the ground carefully and deliberately rolling it into being flat 
on the ground.

1. Lift your foot high, sweeping it back and forth, searching for anything that 
you may disturb that could make noise. 
2. Begin to place the foot on the ground toes first.

edge.

While you are walking like this, you must constantly scan the area and listen 
for any sound you are making as you move. Again, the goal is to be silent, not 
quick.

to your advantage. Even in deserts and prairies, you can use high and low 
spots to move without detection.

source_components.text:
34 
34 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• Never crest a hill or ridge. Instead, move around the side to avoid 
silhouetting yourself. 
• Use creeks and streams to mask the sound of your movement. If your 
footfalls are being masked or not making a lot of noise, you can forego 
ghost-walking and walk at a quicker pace. 
• Use the low ground to avoid detection from observers, but periodically 
move to positions to get eyes on the high ground to potentially spot 
anyone who may observe you. 
• When you have to move in the open, stay as low as possible and 
minimize the amount of time you are exposed.  
• Move from cover to cover. 
Take The Road Less Traveled 
Humans are lazy by nature, and we like to take the easy path whenever we can. 
Any woodland area with a lot of human activity has a network of trails that 
follow the most accessible routes. Even animals like to follow the easy path and 
game trails are often the least difficult. While using well-travelled trails can be 
helpful to move rapidly, they also open us up to a significant amount of risk.  
To combat this, we can avoid any paths that appear to be well -travelled, but 
there are problems in doing this. The first being that the road less travelled is 
often less travelled for a reason. The terrain and vegetation may be too difficult 
to move quickl y, and the foliage may cause silent movement to be effectively 
impossible. 
A better solution is to use a hybrid of the two. For example, use the terrain that 
is not well travelled to conceal yourself and use the pathways that allow easy 
travel to move quickly through an area in short intervals.  
Only do so when you are sure that the odds of detection are low, and you can 
be alerted to people on the trail before they see you, giving yourself enough 
time to move off and let them pass. 
Avoid using game trails because they will attract hunters who will notice 
human tracks, alerting them to another person in the area.

35 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
There is a technique for stepping on and off the main trails. Take the largest, 
most exaggerated step off the path that you can. Pick an area with something 
that you can step behind that will hide any tracks that you may leave after you 
step off the trail that may be visible to trackers. Also, when selecting a spot to 
step off, ensure the trail itself is not in such a state that it holds tracks well. The 
same is true of stepping onto the path.  
After you step off the trail, you should move parallel to the path for a way back 
along the way you came. Find an area to stop and observe the trail to make sure 
that you are not being followed. Also, before stepping onto a trail, conduct a 
five-minute listening halt to make sure the trail is clear. 
When to Abandon Your Vehicle 
In many emergency situations, a vehicle can help you cover ground quickly and 
carry more supplies than you could on foot. However, there comes a point 
where a vehicle becomes a liability rather than an advantage. Recognizing when 
to abandon your vehicle is  critical to maintaining mobility and avoiding 
detection. 
Vehicles are limited to roads and established paths. If those routes become 
blocked, monitored, or dangerous, staying with your vehicle may expose you to 
unnecessary risk. A stalled or disabled vehicle can also trap you in place and 
make you an easy target. 
There are several indicators that it may be time to abandon your vehicle. These 
include blocked or heavily congested roads, visible checkpoints, increased 
human activity, or terrain that your vehicle cannot traverse. Mechanical failure 
or lack of fuel will also force this decision. 
Before leaving your vehicle, you should take only what is essential. Prioritize 
your bug -out bag, water, food, medical supplies, and any critical equipment. 
Avoid overloading yourself, as excessive weight will slow you down and 
increase fatigue. 
When transitioning to foot movement, move away from roads and obvious 
travel routes as quickly as possible. Use terrain features such as low ground,

36 
36 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
vegetation, and natural cover to conceal your movement. Apply the same 
principles of stealth, noise discipline, and movement techniques covered earlier 
in this book. 
If time allows, take steps to reduce the likelihood that your vehicle will draw 
attention to your direction of travel. Avoid leaving obvious signs of where you 
went after abandoning it. 
Once on foot, your priorities shift to remaining undetected, conserving energy, 
and maintaining a steady pace. A vehicle may get you part of the way, but your 
ability to move quietly and efficiently on foot will determine your chances of 
success. 
Listening Halts 
Every so often, you should stop moving and spend at least five minutes 
listening to your surroundings. You and your group should be silent during 
this process. Once you are sure that the area is free of anything or anyone who 
may discover you, you can resume movement. 
Water Sources on the Move 
While moving through the outdoors, maintaining access to water is one of your 
highest priorities. Dehydration will quickly reduce your ability to think clearly, 
move efficiently, and remain aware of your surroundings. 
Finding water on the move requires understanding how water flows through the 
terrain. Low ground, valleys, and natural depressions are more likely to contain 
water than high ground. Streams and rivers are obvious sources, but smaller 
indicators such as damp soil, dense vegetation, or the presence of animal tracks 
can also lead you to water.

36 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
vegetation, and natural cover to conceal your movement. Apply the same 
principles of stealth, noise discipline, and movement techniques covered earlier 
in this book. 
If time allows, take steps to reduce the likelihood that your vehicle will draw 
attention to your direction of travel. Avoid leaving obvious signs of where you 
went after abandoning it. 
Once on foot, your priorities shift to remaining undetected, conserving energy, 
and maintaining a steady pace. A vehicle may get you part of the way, but your 
ability to move quietly and efficiently on foot will determine your chances of 
success. 
Listening Halts 
Every so often, you should stop moving and spend at least five minutes 
listening to your surroundings. You and your group should be silent during 
this process. Once you are sure that the area is free of anything or anyone who 
may discover you, you can resume movement. 
Water Sources on the Move 
While moving through the outdoors, maintaining access to water is one of your 
highest priorities. Dehydration will quickly reduce your ability to think clearly, 
move efficiently, and remain aware of your surroundings. 
Finding water on the move requires understanding how water flows through the 
terrain. Low ground, valleys, and natural depressions are more likely to contain 
water than high ground. Streams and rivers are obvious sources, but smaller 
indicators such as damp soil, dense vegetation, or the presence of animal tracks 
can also lead you to water.

37 
37 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Moving water is generally safer than stagnant water, but no natural source should 
be assumed safe without treatment. Even clear water can contain bacteria, 
parasites, or other contaminants that can cause serious illness. 
Because of this, you must always have a method of purification that is compact 
and easy to use while on the move. Boiling water is one of the most reliable 
methods, but it may not always be practical if you are trying to remain 
undetected. In these situations, filtration systems or purification tablets provide a 
faster and more discreet solution. 
When collecting water, minimize your exposure. Avoid spending unnecessary 
time at the source, especially in open areas where you may be visible. If possible, 
collect water quickly and move to a concealed location before treating and storing 
it. 
Water sources can also attract both animals and people, increasing the risk of 
detection. Always observe the area before approaching and remain alert while 
collecting water. 
Always carrying a small amount of water, along with a reliable purification 
method, allows you to stay mobile without depending entirely on known sources. 
The goal is to maintain a steady supply without slowing your movement or 
exposing your position. 
Communication 
If you are trying to disappear with a group, you will need to communicate 
amongst the group by speaking as little as possible. Fortunately, there are many 
ways that you can communicate in virtual silence with other group members.

This is not an exhaustive list, and you should add more hand signals that you 
can agree upon with your group members. 
➢ Halt 
Hold your non-dominant hand up with palm facing forward and elbow bent at 
90 degrees. 
➢ Move/Deploy

46 
46 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Communicating Through Voice 
If you must speak to a group member, only do so in a whisper through a cupped 
hand over the top of the person's ear. If the environment has a lot of background 
noise, such as running water, then you can exercise more freedom in 
communication through your voice.  
However, at all times, you should never speak above a whisper which should be 
quiet enough that it would be impossible to make out what you are saying from 
even a few meters away. 
How to Cross Checkpoints Without Getting 
Stopped 
In many situations, you may be forced to pass through controlled areas such as 
checkpoints, roadblocks, or zones where movement is being monitored. These 
locations are designed to identify threats, control movement, and gather 
information. Approaching them incorrectly can draw attention and put you at 
risk. 
The first rule when dealing with checkpoints is to avoid them whenever 
possible. If there is a safe alternative route, it is almost always better to use it. 
However, when avoidance is not an option, how you behave becomes critical. 
Your appearance should match the environment and the expectations of those 
controlling the checkpoint. Clothing, equipment, and overall presentation 
should not stand out or raise suspicion. Anything that looks out of place will 
draw attention. 
Movement and body language are just as important as appearance. You should 
move in a calm and deliberate manner, avoiding sudden movements or 
behavior that could be interpreted as nervous or evasive. Confidence without 
aggression is key.

source_components.text:
47 
47 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Keep your actions simple and predictable. Do not volunteer unnecessary 
information and only respond to what is asked. The more you say, the more 
opportunities there are for inconsistencies or suspicion. 
Timing can also play a role. Moving during periods of higher activity may allow 
you to blend in more easily, while isolated movement can attract attention. 
Observing the checkpoint from a distance before approaching can provide 
valuable information about patterns, behavior, and potential risks. 
If you are carrying equipment, ensure that it is organized and does not appear 
threatening or unusual. Anything that draws attention may result in further 
inspection. 
The goal is not to deceive through complex actions, but to avoid standing out. 
Blending into the expected flow of people and maintaining controlled, natural 
behavior will reduce the likelihood of being stopped or questioned. 
Communicating Through Radio 
Using radio to communicate will become problematic since their use is almost 
entirely dependent on us using our voices to speak into the radio. In addition, 
speakers on radios can be loud as well, which will give your position away.  
One way to combat the speaker giving away your position is to use earpieces 
instead of the built -in speakers. Most of these earpieces will also include a 
microphone so that you can position close to your mouth.

48 
48 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
In situations where you do not want to speak into the radio, you can instead key 
the push to talk button momentarily, which will cause the other radios on the 
same frequency to break squelch briefly. You can designate a meaning based on 
the number of times the squelch is broken in a row.  
As an example: 
Break Squelch Three Times = Meet at the rendezvous 
Break Squelch Twice = Approaching camp 
Break Squelch Once = Danger or stay still 
Keep the volume at the lowest level that allows for effective communication, 
and make sure that the LED display will not illuminate when you are 
transmitting. 
Rally Point Protocol 
If you are moving with a group or your family, there is always the possibility 
that you may become separated. In a high -stress situation, confusion, terrain, 
and limited visibility can quickly split even well -organized groups apart. 
Without a plan, this can lead to panic and poor decision-making. 
A rally point protocol ensures that separated individuals can regroup without 
needing to rely on communication devices that may fail or give away your 
position. 
Before moving into any area, you should establish at least one primary rally 
point and one or more secondary rally points. These locations should be easy 
to identify but not obvious to others who may be in the area. 
A good rally point should be easy for your group to recognize, while also being 
located away from roads, trails, and other high -traffic areas. It needs to be 
defensible and provide adequate concealment, and it should be accessible from 
multiple directions to allow flexibility in movement. 
In addition to choosing the location, you must also establish timing. Decide how 
long each person should wait at the rally point before moving on to the next

49 
49 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
one. This prevents people from waiting too long in one place and risking 
detection. 
If radios are available, simple signals can be used to coordinate movement. For 
example: 
Break squelch three times = Move to the rally point 
However, you should never rely entirely on communication devices. A 
predetermined plan is far more reliable. 
Each member of the group must understand the plan fully. If even one person 
is unsure of the rally points or timing, the system can fail. 
The goal is simple: if you become separated, there is no confusion about where 
to go or what to do. Everyone follows the same plan, and the group comes back 
together without unnecessary risk. 
Light Discipline 
During the nighttime hours, it is imperative to keep your use of artificial light 
to a minimum. Sometimes this may be unavoidable, especially when you need 
to do tasks like consulting a map. However, there are a few rules for the use of 
light in situations where your goal is to remain undetected: 
• Avoid the use of white light at all costs. Have a red and blue color filter 
for your flashlight and headlamps. You want two colors of filters because 
under a red filter, the color red will not be visible, and likewise, under a 
blue filter, the color blue will not show up. Switch these filters depending 
on which colors that you need to be able to see.  
• There are instances when you need to perform first -aid, and using a red 
filter will hurt your efforts. You need to use white light to see bleeding 
effectively in these situations, so use the lowest brightness setting 
possible.

Break squelch three times = Move to the rally point 
However, you should never rely entirely on communication devices. A 
predetermined plan is far more reliable. 
Each member of the group must understand the plan fully. If even one person 
is unsure of the rally points or timing, the system can fail. 
The goal is simple: if you become separated, there is no confusion about where 
to go or what to do. Everyone follows the same plan, and the group comes back 
together without unnecessary risk. 
Light Discipline 
During the nighttime hours, it is imperative to keep your use of artificial light 
to a minimum. Sometimes this may be unavoidable, especially when you need 
to do tasks like consulting a map. However, there are a few rules for the use of 
light in situations where your goal is to remain undetected: 
• Avoid the use of white light at all costs. Have a red and blue color filter 
for your flashlight and headlamps. You want two colors of filters because 
under a red filter, the color red will not be visible, and likewise, under a 
blue filter, the color blue will not show up. Switch these filters depending 
on which colors that you need to be able to see.  
• There are instances when you need to perform first -aid, and using a red 
filter will hurt your efforts. You need to use white light to see bleeding 
effectively in these situations, so use the lowest brightness setting 
possible.

outdoors remaining undetected, you will need to consider how you will clean 
your body. Staying clean helps you to remain invisible because it reduces 
unmistakable human body odor.  
There are a few tips and tricks to clean yourself while hiding in the bush 
effectively: 
• Only use unscented soap, deodorant, and toothpaste. 
• Wash and powder your feet daily. If the tactical situation allows for it, air 
your boots every day. 
• Wash your body by giving yourself a sponge bath or finding a secluded 
body of water to bathe. Be sure that any soap that you use is all -natural 
and biodegradable. 
Clean Your Clothes 
When your goal is to remain undetected in the outdoors, it may seem that 
washing one's clothes would not be a priority. But, on the contrary, keeping 
your clothes as clean as practical is essential to keeping your odor under 
control.  
Washing your clothes while trying to be invisible is very difficult. When you are 
trying to remain undetected, the best practice is to be ready to leave at a 
moment's notice. This means that your kit should be squared away so that you 
can grab your gear and withdraw from the area within seconds. If you have half 
of your clothing hung up air drying, bugging out becomes more troublesome.  
Also, the lack of a fire to dry your clothing makes doing laundry a far more 
arduous task. To combat this, we need to wash our clothing in small batches. 
Focus on cleaning undergarments rather than your outer layers; since the next 
of skin layers will take  on the most sweat, and in turn, body odors, they will 
contribute the most to our stinkiness.

52 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
forgo washing your clothes, but you will need to keep your clothing clean in any 
longer-term survival situation. 
Mind The Wind 
Any hunter will tell you that the wind is one of the driving factors preventing 
your prey from detecting you. The same can be said for any people who may be 
looking to locate you. The problem is that you cannot control where the wind 
blows, and while you will want to move into the wind so that anyone ahead of 
you will not smell you, anyone following you will be treated to whatever funky 
odors you've managed to generate.  
No Cooking 
If you want to be invisible, you cannot cook food. The act of even warming 
food up will cause the odors of that food to be carried along with the breeze 
towards people that you potentially do not want to discover you and your 
camp. So instead, eat food that requires no preparation and is wrapped in 
packaging that you can open quietly. 
Bury Your Human Waste  
We all have to void our bowels as a course of daily living. As we try to be 
invisible in the woods, we need to bury that waste deep enough to eliminate the 
smell, and there is no possibility of our makeshift toilet being discovered. 
Leaving No Trace 
If someone is actively tracking you, take steps to ensure that you leave as close 
to zero traces of your presence as possible. Doing this will be very challenging 
and require a significant amount of discipline to pull off.

54 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
▪ Loose dirt will hold the evidence of your tracks to a lesser extent but 
will still show where you stepped. 
▪ You may track materials from one area to another that could seem out 
of place. As an example, you may have a piece of moss stuck to the sole 
of your boot that may come loose in a rocky area where it is very 
apparent that it found its way there from another location. 
▪ Rocks that are moved will often have an indent in the earth where the 
stone was previously. Likewise, trampling plants or grass will leave an 
undeniable sign that you were moving through an area. 
What can we do to minimize the tracks that we leave as we move? 
▪  Avoid walking in muddy areas. Try to box around them wherever 
possible. If you must move through a muddy area, try to step into 
existing tracks if possible. 
▪  Use travel corridors that are heavily travelled to mask your 
movements. This is a 
counterintuitive procedure to 
take from the standpoint of 
remaining undetected. Still, it can 
be beneficial as you move through 
an area step onto a trail or path 
with many competing tracks and 
signs. Move along this path for a 
distance, then step off the path by 
taking a giant step in such a way that anyone who is tracking you will 
not be able to see where you stepped off. 
▪ Be careful not to disturb anything on the ground as you walk. 
▪ Do not walk-through high grass as this will leave a trail where you 
were moving.

55 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Covering Our Tracks 
Covering our tracks rarely works as well as we intend. What we see in the 
movies in the way of brushing our tracks away with a leafy branch or trying to 
walk backwards are methods that may fool inexperienced trackers. However, 
anyone who is knowledgeable and experienced in the art of tracking will not 
be fooled. It is better to make an effort to leave as few tracks as possible than 
to try and erase any tracks that you do leave. Depending on who is tracking 
you, it may be a better strategy to move faster than those who are in pursuit 
rather than make attempts to trick them.  
Garbage 
Do not leave any trash behind. It sounds simple and an obvious aspect of being 
invisible in the outdoors, but the issue is, policing your garbage is a lot more 
complicated than we would suspect.  
Every wrapper, piece of paper, human excrement, shell casing, and uneaten 
food must be accounted for and 
either carried with you or buried 
deep enough that there is no 
possibility of it being uncovered 
accidentally. 
One way trash can be accidentally 
left behind is when a wrapper or 
other bits of debris is inside your 
pocket. As your hand moves in and 
out of the pocket, there is always the 
probability of a piece of rubbish falling from the pocket onto the ground without 
you noticing it.  
The best way to combat this is to carry a ziplock bag in which you place all the 
trash you produce. A bag of that size is far more challenging to lose accidentally 
than a crumpled-up gum wrapper.

56 
56 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Foodstuffs 
In any survival or off -grid scenario, you should be leaving no food uneaten. 
However, if you find yourself with portions of food that have not been 
consumed, do not discard them into the bush or attempt to bury them. Instead, 
carry them with you in the sam e way that you transport your food. This 
includes the packaging of the food as well.  
Human Waste 
Human excrement will be a big sign that you are in an area because you cannot 
stop yourself from voiding your bowels. Even urine can lead to your detection 
if it is fresh enough where the odor is still hanging in the air, or the liquid is 
pooled on the ground or has made the vegetation or soil wet. The best way to 
avoid having your bowel movements give away your location is to carry them 
with you double bagged. However, this is an extreme measure and not one that 
everyone will want or need to do. The alternative is to bury your waste deep 
enough that it will not be discovered, and i n such a way, there is little to no 
evidence that the ground was disturbed. 
Shell Casings 
Depending on the situation, you may find yourself having to discharge a 
firearm. You must retrieve the shell casing for every round of ammunition you 
expend if you want to stay as invisible as possible.  
Shelter Areas 
It is almost impossible to shelter in an area and not leave any sign that we were 
sleeping there. There are a few things that we can do to minimize our impact 
on the site, though:

57 
57 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
• Choose a shelter site and sleeping area that will result in minimal 
disruption in the ground, leaving as little sign as possible that someone 
slept there. 
• Do not build a fire. Not only does a fire betray you through the light and 
smoke it produces but erasing the existence of a fire pit from the ground 
is almost impossible. 
• Move around the area as little as possible. Every step that you take leaves 
sign. 
Supply Cache Strategy 
If you are forced to move over long distances, carrying everything you need on 
your back is not always practical. Weight slows you down, increases fatigue, 
and makes it harder to remain undetected. 
A supply cache strategy allows you to pre-position essential supplies along your 
route so that you can travel lighter while still having access to critical resources 
when needed. 
A cache is simply a hidden store of supplies placed in advance. These can 
include food, water, clothing, medical supplies, or equipment that you may need 
later. 
When selecting a cache location, you should choose an area that is difficult to 
stumble upon accidentally, easy for you to relocate using terrain features, away 
from common travel routes, and protected from the elements. 
Caches should be concealed carefully. Burying them is one option, but you must 
take care to leave minimal disturbance to the ground. Another option is to hide 
supplies under natural cover such as logs, rocks, or dense vegetation. 
Waterproof containers should always be used to protect the contents from 
moisture and environmental damage.

58 
58 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
It is also important to avoid placing all your supplies in a single location. 
Multiple smaller caches reduce the risk of losing everything if one is discovered. 
When using a cache, approach the area carefully and observe it from a distance 
before moving in. If the cache site appears disturbed or compromised, do not 
approach it. 
A well-planned cache system allows you to move faster, carry less weight, and 
extend your operational range without sacrificing essential supplies. 
Invisible Shelter Options 
No matter the tactical situation, we will need some form of shelter to protect 
ourselves from the elements. Unfortunately, good shelter sites can be hard to 
find when you are not trying to be invisible, so when you want to shelter 
undetected, you are more than likely to have to settle for shelter sites that are 
less than desirable. 
Site Selection 
The key here is to select a shelter location that no one is going to stumble upon 
accidentally. This means that it has to be far removed from any populated areas, 
roads, paths, or game trails. Beyond that, you will also want to enter and exit

source_components.text:
59 
59 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
from the shelter site at points that are not visible from anyone who would care 
to notice. 
The best practice would be to have a significant amount of brush and shrub 
between yourself and anyone who would be looking for you. Along with this, 
you could choose a shelter site that is overly difficult to access or that has entry 
and exit points that you can camouflage effectively.  
One example would be to have shrubs or brush that you could place at the 
entrances and exits, which can quickly move out of the way.  
Alternatively, you could select an area that you could enter and exit from that 
has vegetation that appears to be challenging to negotiate but that you and your 
group members can slip through relatively quickly. 
Entry And Exit Points 
Never use the same point to both enter and exit the shelter site. If you are being 
pursued, the highest likelihood of your shelter being discovered is through the 
point that you enter it.  
Therefore, this point should be as concealed as practical and observable from 
the shelter site. The best-case scenario is to place a few early warning devices 
at this point so that if your site is compromised, you can make a hasty exit. 
As for exit points, you should never rely on only one. Instead, there must be 
several exit routes so that you and your group members can escape in seconds 
through different ways, rendezvousing later at a predetermined point.

60 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Shelter Types 
Any shelter that you use has to be able to be deployed and collapsed in minutes. 
Constructing something out of natural materials will never be a good option if 
you are trying to remain undetected. The act of gathering the wood for the 
shelter alone will mean that 
you will leave many signs 
around the area.  
For myself personally, I like 
to use a standard eight -foot 
by eight-foot square tarp that 
I pitch at a very shallow angle 
to keep it as low to the 
ground as I possibly can. The 
style of tarp shelter you 
choose matters less than the 
overall height of the shelter.  
The goal is to have the shelter be 
low enough to the ground that 
brush, shrubs, and other 
vegetation can do a good job 
concealing it from view without 
you having to take the time and 
effort to camouflage the actual 
tarp. 
It may be a good idea to use a 
piece of low ground to set your 
tarp shelter over but be aware that water and cold air will be collecting in the 
low ground, so in certain areas, this may not be an appropriate shelter site.

61 
61 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Staying Aware 
If you are hiding in the woods, you are on the defensive and, in turn, need to 
think about how you are going to spot someone approaching your shelter 
before they spot you. The best way to do this is to use early warning devices, 
but posting a sentry is also good practice when more than one person is hiding 
in the woods. Regardless of how you will be warned of impending danger, you 
also should be orienting your shelter to have a view of the most likely avenues 
of ingress by people you are trying to be invisible from. 
Hiding From Thermal Vision 
Devices 
One of the most difficult methods of detection to hide from are thermal imagers. 
These devices are used in helicopters and drones, can be mounted on vehicles, 
and have become small enough to be portable and easy to deploy in a wide 
variety of locations. Thermal imaging is typically used by the military and law 
enforcement but has found its way into the civilian market in recent years. 
Defeating thermal imaging is very difficult and unfortunately cannot be done in 
such a way as to conceal oneself fully. Still, we can mask our infrared signature 
enough to limit any observer's ability to pick our signature out of the 
background. 
How Does Thermal Imaging Work? 
A thermal imager detects the infrared radiation that everything above zero 
degrees Kelvin emits. Once the camera detects the infrared radiation, it 
translates it into an image demonstrating the difference in temperature 
between the objects in the camera's field of view. The imager can display a 
colorized image or a black and white image depending on the type and purpose 
of the unit.

63 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
though, which means that fog could be used as cover as long as there is 
sufficient distance between yourself and the observer. 
• Thermal vision is effectively night vision, so the cover of darkness is no 
match for a thermal imager. 
Best Practices For Avoiding Detection By 
Thermal Vision Devices 
While there are things that you can do to hide from thermal vision, there are 
also a few things that you should do first to avoid detection from thermal 
imagers. If you suspect that there are areas under surveillance through thermal 
vision, you should avoi d those areas as the first line of defense. If you cannot 
avoid areas that may be under surveillance by thermal imaging or if you are 
attempting to evade drones, there are a few things that you can do to reduce 
your odds of being discovered. 
• Thermal imaging cannot see through tree trunks, but it can be used to 
pick out heat signatures within forested areas. When moving through 
forested areas, stay close to the trunks of trees and move from cover to 
cover swiftly. Avoid treelines and open spaces, and when you find places 
that offer concealment, exploit them to your fullest advantage.  
• Avoid moving at night when there is a threat of detection from thermal 
imaging. Instead, move during the daylight hours when there will be 
many more heat signatures to blend with.  
• Only move when necessary. Staying still undercover will keep you hidden 
far better than if you decide to move from place to place.

64 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
How To Shield Yourself From Detection By 
Thermal Imaging 
There are not a lot of good options for shielding oneself from thermal cameras. 
However, we can try and block or diffuse our heat signatures in the hopes that 
it will make our heat signatures more challenging to spot.  
Blocking Infrared 
There are a couple of ways to block infrared radiation that are field expedient.  
The first is to build a shelter that has thick walls and overhead cover. The 
walls will help to mask your signature, and the overhead cover will diffuse the 
radiation that leaks from the shelter. This is an excellent option for a 
permanent shelter setup or a semi-permanent shelter but not a good option if 
you will be on the move.  
Mylar emergency blankets can be used to block the heat that our body emits 
and should be used to line a shelter or to cover ourselves. The big problem with 
mylar blankets is that they are shiny or colored with bright colors. Some styles 
are green in color, and these would be better to use.

65 A GREEN BERET'S BUG-OUT GUIDE 
Wool blankets can also be used to cover oneself with or use as overhead cover 
for your shelter. Using heavy wool blankets is a strategy that the Taliban have 
used to avoid detection by thermal imaging by Allied forces 
Wear insulated clothing to keep the heat from escaping into the surrounding 
air. Your exposed skin will still show up on thermal imagers, but your body will 
be less noticeable. 
Diffusing Infrared 
When blocking infrared is not possible or practical, you can take some 
measures to diffuse your heat signature. 
Camouflage netting will still allow infrared radiation to escape through the 
holes but block enough of it to lessen your overall heat signature. 
Ghillie suits also diffuse your heat signature.

Consider the following tips: 
• Illuminate all entry points, including front and back doors, garage 
entrances, and windows. Use bright, energy -efficient LED bulbs for 
enhanced visibility. 
• Position lights strategically to eliminate shadows and blind spots 
around your property. 
• Use motion-sensor lights to 
surprise and startle 
potential intruders. This 
sudden activation draws 
attention and increases the 
likelihood of detection. 
• Ensure the lighting fixtures 
are out of reach and 
tamper-proof to prevent criminals from disabling or damaging them. 
• Regularly check and replace burnt -out bulbs to maintain the 
effectiveness of your lighting system. 
• Take note that this may not be viable following an EMP attack or solar 
flare where the power grid has been knocked out, but it is something 
you can do so long as you have power and in your daily life.  
Visible Security Camera Systems 
The presence of visible security measures can significantly deter looters. 
Even experienced criminals will think twice about attempting to rob 
somewhere where they can see security cameras.

source_components.source_label: Documentary page context; adjacent material may be included; image text is not transcribed here
source_components.text:
13 
• Install security cameras at strategic locations, such as near entry 
points, garage areas, and areas with high foot traffic. Opt for cameras 
with high-resolution capabilities and a wide field of view. 
• Ensure the cameras are easily visible from the street and close to 
potential intruders. Place them at eye level or install prominent 
signage indicating the presence of a security system. 
• Connect your security cameras to a digital video recorder (DVR) or a 
cloud-based storage system to store and review the recorded 
footage. This can provide valuable evidence in case of an incident. 
• Consider installing a doorbell camera or a video intercom system to 
visually verify visitors before opening the door. These devices allow 
you to remotely communicate with and see the person at your 
doorstep. 
• Regularly maintain and clean your security cameras to ensure clear 
images and uninterrupted surveillance. 
Reinforced Doors and Windows 
Weak entry points, such as doors and windows, are prime targets for 
looters. The first thing looters will do when they come to your house is look 
for a way to get inside, and while it may sound obvious, most looters will 
attempt to break in through the doors and windows. 
You can deter them by reinforcing your doors and windows so they look 
more difficult to break into.  
Strengthen your doors and windows with the following tips: 
• Use solid core or metal doors for exterior entrances, as they are 
more resistant to forced entry compared to hollow doors.

14 
• Install deadbolt locks with at least a one -inch throw on all exterior 
doors. Choose locks with a hardened steel bolt and an anti -saw pin 
for added security. 
• Consider reinforcing windows with shatterproof glass or security 
film. This film holds the glass together even when broken, making it 
more difficult for looters to gain access. 
• Secure sliding doors 
with a bar or rod in the 
track to prevent forced 
entry. Install a sliding 
door lock or add a 
security bar that 
extends to the floor or 
ceiling. 
• Replace old or worn -
out door and window frames with sturdy materials to enhance their 
resistance against physical attacks. 
Keep in mind that determined looters may come to your door with pry bars, 
sledgehammers, and axes or maul in an attempt to break down your doors. 
Steel doors that are leading outdoors and with heavy duty locks and hinges 
will resist break-ins that normal wooden doors wouldn’t be able to.  
Securing Garage Doors 
The garage often provides an easy entry point for looters, especially when 
all of the other doors and windows have been reinforced like we discussed 
above.

more difficult for looters to gain access. 
• Secure sliding doors 
with a bar or rod in the 
track to prevent forced 
entry. Install a sliding 
door lock or add a 
security bar that 
extends to the floor or 
ceiling. 
• Replace old or worn -
out door and window frames with sturdy materials to enhance their 
resistance against physical attacks.

sledgehammers, and axes or maul in an attempt to break down your doors.

will resist break-ins that normal wooden doors wouldn’t be able to.

• Install a robust locking mechanism on the garage door, such as a

• Keep the garage door closed 
and locked when not in use, 
even if you're just stepping 
away momentarily. Avoid 
leaving the garage door open 
or partially open, as it invites 
unwanted attention. 
• Consider installing a security alarm system specifically designed for 
garage doors. These alarms can detect unauthorized attempts to 
open or tamper with the garage door and trigger an alert. 
• Keep in mind that you should think twice about storing emergency 
supplies for a long-term disaster in your garage. For one thing, a 
garage is not the best environment to store certain essentials such 
as food and water.  
For another thing, a garage door can be fairly easy for looters to break 
into like we mentioned above, and in the event they break in , you 
don’t want to have your critical supplies ripe for the taking as a

• Install door jammers or reinforcement plates to prevent forced entry. 
These devices reinforce the door frame and make it more difficult to 
kick or pry open the door. 
• Use window locks or install window security bars to prevent easy 
access. Window locks should be sturdy and positioned correctly to 
secure the window in a closed position. 
• Consider installing a 
peephole or video doorbell 
to identify visitors before 
opening the door. This 
allows you to verify the 
person's identity without 
compromising your safety. 
• Reinforce glass panels in 
doors with security film or 
laminated glass, making it harder for looters to break the glass and 
gain access. 
Every entry point leading into your home needs to be reinforced. 
Remember, in a grid down disaster scenario looters will want to move 
quickly from home to home to take as much as they can. If they encounter 
any difficulty (thanks to the measures that are l isted above) in attempting 
to break into your home at all, they may disengage and move onto the next 
home.  
Landscaping and Visibility 
You may never have thought of landscaping as being something important 
to do as a prepper, but it is.

17 
That’s because maintaining good visibility around your property can 
discourage looters. Consider these landscaping tips: 
• Trim bushes and hedges near windows and entry points to eliminate 
potential hiding spots for intruders. Keep shrubs below window level 
for an unobstructed view. 
• Choose plants with thorny or prickly foliage near vulnerable areas to 
create a natural deterrent. 
• Keep trees and shrubs well-maintained to enhance visibility from the 
street and neighboring properties. Overgrown vegetation can provide 
cover for looters. 
• Remove any large objects, such as ladders or tools, from your yard 
that could assist intruders in gaining access to your home. 
Valuables Concealment 
Keeping valuable items out of sight can reduce the temptation for burglars.  
Use these strategies: 
• Close blinds or curtains at night to prevent outsiders from peeking 
inside and seeing valuable possessions. Use curtains or blinds that 
are opaque or have a reflective backing for maximum privacy. 
• Avoid displaying expensive items, such as electronics or jewelry, in 
plain view from windows. Store them in secure locations or use 
curtains or blinds to obstruct visibility. 
• Dispose of packaging discreetly, especially for high -value items. 
Break down boxes and place them inside garbage bags to prevent 
potential looters from noticing recent purchases. Consider recycling 
or taking packaging to a recycling center instead of leavi ng it 
curbside.

sensors, motion detectors, and a control panel. Ensure it is 
professionally installed

functionality.

decals to deter potential 
looters. Make it clear that 
your home is protected by 
an active security system. 
• Connect your alarm system to a professional monitoring service for 
immediate response and  notification of authorities in case of a 
triggered alarm. Choose a reputable monitoring company with a 
quick response time. 
By implementing these deterrent strategies, you can significantly reduce 
the chances of your home becoming a target for both criminals in everyday 
life and gangs of looters and marauders following a major grid down 
disaster.

fortifying your home and adding deterrents to looters after a disaster has

1.  Motion-Activated Alarms  
Motion-activated alarms are a game-changer when detecting unexpected 
movement on one's property. These motion-activated alarms can help in 
deterring intruders and enhance overall safety by creating loud noises or 
flashing lights when they detect movements.  
To ensure effective implementation of motion -activated alarms, here are 
some practical tips: 
Strategic Placement 
The key to maximizing the effectiveness of motion-activated alarms lies in 
their strategic placement. Experts advise installing motion sensors in 
areas where potential intruders are most likely to pass. This includes 
locations near entry points like doors and windows and vulnerable areas 
such as side gates and backyards. Homeowners can significantly increase 
the chances of detecting unauthorized access by focusing on these high -
traffic zones. 
Fine-Tuning Sensitivity 
Fine-tuning the sensitivity of motion sensors is essential to avoid the 
annoyance of false alarms triggered by harmless factors like small animals 
or moving branches. By adjusting the sensitivity levels, homeowners can 
ensure that the alarms are only triggered when necessary. 
Visual Deterrent 
Combining motion-activated alarms with visual deterrents is also a great 
idea. For instance, you can connect bright flood lights or strobe lights. 
When an intruder unknowingly triggers the motion sensors, the sudden 
burst of light startles them, drawing immediate attention to their presence.

2. Window and Door Alarms  
Window and door alarms stand out as a comforting layer of security, 
offering homeowners peace of mind even when they are away or 
asleep.  
Comprehensive Coverage  
Experts stress the importance of comprehensive coverage regarding 
window and door alarms. Attaching these alarms to every accessible 
window and exterior door protects all potential entry points. Often 
overlooked areas like basement windows and side doors c an be 
vulnerable spots for intruders, making it crucial to include them in the 
security plan. 
Audible Alert 
The effectiveness of window and door alarms lies in their ability to act as 
both an alert system for homeowners and a deterrent for potential 
intruders. When triggered, it is best to choose alarms that emit a loud, 
attention-grabbing noise. The piercing so und alerts homeowners to 
potential threats and startles intruders, making them believe they have 
been caught in the act. 
Wireless Convenience 
You should opt for wireless window and door alarms for ease of 
installation and flexibility. These wireless devices can be easily moved

3.  Security Cameras with Motion Detection  
The value of security cameras equipped with motion detection 
capabilities is crucial, as they act as extra vigilant eyes watching over the 
property.  
Strategic Placement 
When it comes to security cameras, strategic placement is key. 
Homeowners are advised to position the cameras to cover all entry points, 
paths leading to the home, and high-traffic areas. By doing so, they ensure 
comprehensive coverage, allowing the camera s to capture valuable 
footage in the event of an incident. 
Real-Time Alerts 
The ability to receive real -time alerts or snapshots on a mobile device 
upon detecting motion is a significant advantage of these security 
cameras. Setting up the cameras to send such alerts is recommended, 
enabling homeowners to act promptly and decisivel y should suspicious 
activity occur. 
Enhanced Night Vision 
Invest in security cameras with advanced night vision capabilities. Clear 
night vision ensures that the cameras can capture essential details even 
in low -light conditions, providing continuous surveillance without 
compromising effectiveness.

4.  Barking Dog Alarms 
Barking dog alarms are a great way to trick the intruder into believing that 
there is an actual presence of a dog and that they need to beware.  
Visible & Audible 
Barking dog alarms are most effective when installed in visible and audible 
locations. Placing these alarms near the front door or in the yard ensures 
potential intruders can hear and see them. The realistic barking sounds 
emitted by these alarms create th e illusion of a vigilant dog, deterring 
intruders from attempting further entry. 
Adjustable Settings 
 To customize the illusion of a dog, homeowners are advised to choose 
barking dog alarms with adjustable settings. These settings may include 
barking volume, frequency, and even the option to simulate the presence 
of a small or large dog. Tailoring these s ettings to match personal 
preferences enhances the effectiveness of the deterrent. 
Integration with Other Alarms 
You can connect barking dog alarms to motion sensors or timers for a 
more comprehensive security approach. By doing so, the alarms can be 
set to activate automatically, adding an extra layer of defense that 
complements other security measures. 
5.  Door Reinforcement Devices

you must use devices that can prevent the intruder from getting in.

 Door jammers and security bars are vital reinforcements for doors, 
making it challenging for intruders to force them open. When properly 
installed, these devices create a physical barrier that can withstand 
significant pressure, providing homeowners with added protection. 
Door Chain & Viewer 
In addition to physical reinforcements, installing a door chain or viewer is 
a great idea. The door chain allows homeowners to partially open the door 
to verify the identity of visitors before granting full access. This simple yet 
effective precaution ensures that only trusted individuals are allowed into 
the home. 
Smart Door Locks 
Upgrading to smart door locks has many advantages, such as remote 
access and monitoring capabilities. With smart locks, homeowners can 
lock or unlock their doors from anywhere, providing greater control and 
convenience over their home security. 
6.  Security Window Film 
The security window film is not just discreet but also a very powerful way 
to improve the security of windows.  
Layer of Protection 
Applying security window film is highly effective in fortifying vulnerable 
windows, such as those on the ground floor or obscured by foliage. This 
specialized film adheres to the glass, making it more resistant to shattering 
and forced entry attempts. 
Hidden Defense

 Door jammers and security bars are vital reinforcements for doors, 
making it challenging for intruders to force them open. When properly 
installed, these devices create a physical barrier that can withstand 
significant pressure, providing homeowners with added protection. 
Door Chain & Viewer 
In addition to physical reinforcements, installing a door chain or viewer is 
a great idea. The door chain allows homeowners to partially open the door 
to verify the identity of visitors before granting full access. This simple yet 
effective precaution ensures that only trusted individuals are allowed into 
the home. 
Smart Door Locks 
Upgrading to smart door locks has many advantages, such as remote 
access and monitoring capabilities. With smart locks, homeowners can 
lock or unlock their doors from anywhere, providing greater control and 
convenience over their home security. 
6.  Security Window Film 
The security window film is not just discreet but also a very powerful way 
to improve the security of windows.  
Layer of Protection 
Applying security window film is highly effective in fortifying vulnerable 
windows, such as those on the ground floor or obscured by foliage. This 
specialized film adheres to the glass, making it more resistant to shattering 
and forced entry attempts.
